WEIMAR, Feb. 6.-One Berlin news
paper has established for the sessions
of the National Assembly the first reg
ular airplane delivery inaugurated on
the Continent. The morning and noon
editions Of this newspaper are deliv-
cred at weimar two hours after pub
lication.


Weimar was filed to-day with tho
most notable throng that probably ever
assembled in the beautiful little Ger
man city. Some 5000 German political
leaders ranging from Chancellor Ebert,
Philip Scheidemann. Count Won
Brockdorff- antzau. the Foreign Sec
retary, and Matthias Erzberger to the
humblest and hitherto unknown fig

empire have been gradually gathering
here and are ready for the opening to-

Special trains for the last two days

been made that virtually every one
who arrived received eating and sleep
ing accommodations by nightfall yes
terday.

Weimar fortunately possesses an un-
usual number OF good. although small
hotels. Virtually all were requisitioned
by the authorities. They took similar
action in the case of many private
houses and spare rooms in homes.


The Weimar "Wohnungsrath," or resi-
dence bureau. thea took up the task and
allotted living quarters TO specified
groups, such as the Ministerial party.
the members OF the Assembly and the
correspondents, keeping each group
together as nearly as possible. The
bureau after assigning the visitors to
the hotels where they will live for the
next several weeks designated eating
places.


These places were divided into three
classes-the better hotels and pensions
where the luncheon costs moro than Ave
marks and the supper more than four
marks the hotels and pensions where
the meals cost from three and one-half
TO five marks and the smaller eating
places where the prices range from two
marks to three marks fifty pfennig


Each guest is obliged to eat at the
place assigned TO him. for the hotels are
under the strictest orders to furnish with
food and lodging only those guests who
present the proper card calling for such
service.

And scented English lanes:
They loved the sunlight on their downs
And the soft English rains.
And nOw-they sleep in Flanders
or where the sad Marine flows,
A bleak white cross above their heads;
Their names, ah. no one knows!
They loved the life of London.
With lights that cleaned like pearls.
And thcaters and taYerns

Their youth was n brief glory
That sped too swiftly by:
They left their schools and cricket
And came out hereto die.
And some were shining poets,
And some We're simple boys
Who loved the Surrey fields and all
Substantial English joys.
From Elton and from oxford.
From many an English town.
They came to save world from shame
And lay their young lives down.
In some celestial garden


Perhaps they sit today
And laugh as once they used to laugh,
Play as they used to play.

But they-they are not dead,
Though simple crosses stand above
Each brave young English head.
They loved and are contented
On windy wastes to sleep.
Yet when the English daisies
Begin to smile and creep,
Pluck them and take them over
To many a lonely grave:
For they loved English flowers.

What shall do to prevent the
damage done by those blackish brown
bugs about an inch long that seem
both to suck the sap and poison the
squash vines?-J. H. s., Duchess
county. New York.


When the bugs appear in spring
have some squash plants ready for
them to feed on-not the ones you
count on yourself. but "any old"
squash plants-a thick clump here and
another there. When the bugs are
busy sucking in the early morning
spray them with pure kerosene. This
will kill them. probably also the plants.
Do this with different clumps on diff
ferent days until the squashes you
want to save begin to sprout. Under
the leaves of these plants place chips,
leaves, bits Of tin and other things
for the bugs to shelter beneath at
night In the morning gather the
adults and drop them into kerosene or
tramp on them. Look sharp for others
on the plants and treat them the same
way. When you find golden brown
round eggs CASUALLY on the under sides
OF the leaves) cut out the clusters and
tramp on them. They are easily seen.
When the young bugs hatch from eggs
that you have missed spray the under
sides of the leaves thoroughly with
kerosene emulsion diluted with about
eight times as much water. This will
kill them, but not the adults. In the
fall when the vines are killed by frost
leave the immature squashes in the
field. visit them every day or so and
knock off the bugs that congregate
upon them. Either tramp on them or
dump them into kerosene. This Will
reduce the number that would other
wise live over winter.

MOUNT CLEMENS, Mich,
49, Aug. 15.-The amount of
costs that Henry Ford may re-
ceive from the Chicago Daily
Tribune. in addition to the six
cents damages awarded him last
night by a jury, which heard his
libel suit against the Chicago
newspaper, will not exceed $50.
Under a Michigan law where
nominal damages are awarded,
not more than $50 costs can be
assessed against the losing party.


Alfred Lucking, senior counsel
for Mr.. Ford, said this morning
that little attention had been
given to the matter Of costs and
that until he had looked up the
law covering the case, he could
not say how much the plaintiff
could expect to receive. Among
other attorneys, however, the
opinion was held that In cases
where damages awarded amount
to less than $50, the costs col
lectible may not exceed the judg-
ment awarded. In this event,
Mr.. Ford could demand only six
cents costs from the Tribune.

ST. JOHNS, N. F., May 25-The
Donaldson liner Cassandra, which
struck an iceberg 100 miles off Cape
Race, arrived here tonight. The 400
passengers aboard are well. The hull
is damaged forward.


The ship sent out wireless calls for
assistance day, and it was feared at
first that she was sinking


The vessel struck a submerged sec
tion of the berg. Immediately passen-
gers and crew were called to quarters
and the ships boats swung out. Pas
sengers were escorted to deck with
but slight confusion. There was no
excitement, according to the ships
officers, who stated the damage was
limited to springing Of several plates on
the starboard side below the water
line abaft amidships. The ship made
little or no water, and after sending
out calls for help came here at top
speed.


The Cassandra had been stopped all
night in the heavy fog, :nd at dawn
the steamer was put under way again.


The grating sound of the hull scrap
ing on the submerged ledge caused
orders for full speed astern. Passen-
gers not yet up were not awakened by
the accident but were called later.


The berg was described as tower
ing, with ledge just below the water
line. The waters in the vicinity of
Cape Race, on the North of Ireland
track followed by the Cassandra, are
thick with bergs, according to the Cas-
sandra's officers.


Although early reports were to the
effect that hole was stove in the
ships side, it was stated tonight that
the chief reason for stopping here was
to obtain a survey before proceeding
overseas.


MONTREAL, May 25.-The Cas-
sandra was able to make port under
her own power after the crew had made
temporary repairs at sea, according to
advices received here tonight.


The liner registers $3.50 tons gross.
She left here for Glasgow last Wednes-
day.

by fraternities or university societies

nection with bolshevism. The resolu-
lions also expressed belief in the ne
cessity for continuing the control of
food prices.


James Henry Thomas. labor member
of parliament. acting together with
Robert Smillie, the miners leader.
moved an emergency resolution dep
recating military rule in Ireland, and
declaring that the only solution of
the Irish problem was through the
method of self-determination by
which the Irish people could work
out their own salvation. The resolu-
ton expressed profound sympathy for
the trades unionists' Irish brethren
in their hour of repression This reso-
luton was carried unanimously.

PANAMA, Oct. 5.-Sanitary measures
which have terminated the outbreak of
yellow fever at Guayaquil, Ecuador,
have practically eradicated the yellow
fever scourge from the earth. according
10 Major-Gen. William c. Gorgas,
former Surgeon-General of the. United
States Army. who returned here yester-
day after directing the fight against
yellow fever in West Coast localities.


Gen. Gorgas said that Guayaquil was
the last large centre where yellow fever
had been epidemic and that the nature
OF the disease is such that the few
cases which may occur in small remote
communities will burn out for lack of
incoming persons who are not immune
10 the disease.


No cases of yellow fever have oc-
Cured in Guayaquil in the last three
months owing to the energetic sanitary
measures. Gen. Gorgas said he could
not be certain that the plague was
eradicated there until after the close of
the rainy season. now beginning. but he
thought the sanitary work there was
sufficient to prevent reinfection, bring
Ing about the definite end of the yellow
fever menace. the first of the great
diseases to suffer extirpation.

10 move.


Since the arrival of the American

taken until now by any of the thirty

representatives on the scene.


On Saturday deputation claiming

Serbian delegation, headed by the Serb
ian Premier Pasitch, and including
Serbian, Croatian and Slovene repre-
sentatives.


Three Shiploads of British


Last night the enormous advance
guard of personnel attached to the
British delegation reached Paris. SO
large was the party, which includes
several hundred women stenographers
and secretaries, that three channel
steamers, until lately used as hospital
ships, had to be pressed into service.
Thirty automobiles and motor wagons
met the party at the station and made
several trips before all the baggage
could be moved.


The party was headed by Sir Eyre
Grove and Robert Van Sittart, of the
British Foreign Office. and represent
atives of the India Office. but it is
not believed, since no list has been
made public that any of the British
plenipotentiaries are included.


Arthur Balfour, the British Foreign
Secretary arrived in Paris last week,
hut is spending short holiday in the
Riviera while awaiting Lloyd George
and the other delegates. Edward
Benes the Czecho oSlovak Foreign Min
ister has been here several weeks, and
his colleague, Kramarcz, is expected
daily from Prague.


French Mission Still Secret

official statement that no information
is yet available upon the composition
of the French delegation.


Greece and Serbia, the latter includ

landed at Aberdeen, where complete
overhaul was made before leaving for

WASHINGTON. Aug. 18.-President Fe-

information reached the State Depart
ment to-day. but details have not beer
received. Information that Tinoco had
asked permission of Congress to leave
the country was received here some tim
ago. but It never has been made clear
whether he intended flight or planned to
be absent only a short time.


There also was 10 indication whether
the President quit the country before his
brother, Joaquin Tinoco, Vice-President
was assassinated on August 10.


Departure OF the President and the
killing OF his brother led State Depart
ment officials to hope that the republic
would set up a government which the
United States could recognize.


Tinoco seized the reins of government
through a revolution. and his regime
never was recognized by this country.

An overseas dispatch says two hun

on the desert of what was Vimy
Ridge. This is the beginning of the
proposed Canadian memorial forest
the maple is Canada's emblematic
tree-and the saplings just placed are
declared to be the only living trees In
the war zone today.


How the landscape has been
changed, and how the reconstructed
one will differ from that before the
war! Most Americans think OF Hol-
land, Belgium. Flanders as painted by
Van Goyen. Ruyysdael. Rembrandt
and others. 1nstinctlveiy the men'I
picture follows Hobbema's avenue of
Middleharnis," with spindling. thin
shanked, wisp-topped and scant-on-
shade trees either side the road. What
a different aspect naples would give
the scene, or oaks. or elms or other
wide-spreading varieties. The Euro
pean. like the oriental. seems to have
chosen his favorite trees on some 9TH
er basis than expansive foliage-the
cedar, the cypress. the palm, the
stonepine, the poplar of Lombardy;
vet the inspiration for Gothic cathe-
drals came from the solemn groves of
arch-like trunks and limbs and foli-
age, and wherever two elms meet
there is the suggestion right at hand.


Many years must elapse before the
war-torn regions are again venerable
with trees and by that time a new
school of landscape painting may have
come, glad to paint full, rounded trees
like the American. Inness; or, revers-
ing the Inness method of leaving
circular opening through his trees to
reveal the scene beyond, this future
school may feature the transplanted
naples rounded "area" in the fore=
ground while displaying the Euro
pean background on either side.

Wilson probably today, but beyond

conferences here the Secretary and
his party will visit Italy and parts
of the fighting fronts in France, and
then will go to England.

CALGARY, Alberta, March 3.-General
snowfalls covering all Alberta have i'm
proved the agricultural outlook i'm
mensely during the last week. The
ground was 80 dry when winter set In
that II could not freeze. Coupled with
this was continued mild weather until
ten days ago. when the first zero tenn
peratures OF the year were recorded, and
with the low temperatures came heavy
snowfslls. When this snow melts the
moisture will sink deep into the soil
and will furnish excellent seed bed and
assure termination.


This will mean probably larger seeded
areas. This reassuring condition has
had an immediate and substantial effect
on business. which. fairly brisk before.
had taken a decided upturr.


Seasonable winter goods are selling
well. and the coal trade has received an
impetus that will enable it at least to
break even and perhaps make little
profit.


Sub-zero temperatures have been re-
corded for almost a fortnight. The Do
minion and Federal governments are in
creasing their estimates for public works
and railways, and there will be nc
dearth Of employment when spring
comes.


The present situation Is not in the
least critical. Increased land settlement
will improve the agricultural machinery
business and the main trouble may be
the obtaining OF enough implements.
Generally speaking. the outlook may
be regarded as highly satisfactory, and
the usual June rains will mean heavy
crops all through the harvest area.

NEW YORK. December 20.-Rallies
from the recent decentralization in for
eign exchange. easier rates for call
money and a concerted drive against
the shorts in some Of the popular
speculative issues effected sharp re-
covery of prices in the stock market
this week.


The rebound lacked uniformity,
however, rails. for example, holding
back on the unsatisfactory status of
federal legislation and the attitude OF
organized labor respecting the return
of the railroads to private owners.


Trading in the early days Of the
week was comparatively dull and
often without definite tendencies, but
extensive purchases Of oils. motors
and the usual leaders among steels
and equipme ents elevated average quo
tations materially at the end.


All classes of industrials were
stimulated by the enormous demand
for finished products in steel. and iron
and coppers were moderately respon-
sive to large exports and higher prices
for the refined metal.


The Supreme Court decision sus-
tanning wartime prohibition, and the
agreement entered into by the big
packers with the government to with
draw from all outside business except
dairy products, exerted only tempo
rary effect upon the general financial
situation.

GENEVA, Sept. Five Hungarian SOL
diers. prisoners OF war who escaped
from Italy, recently entered Switzerland
across the mountain pass "Aiguilles
vertes," more than 10000 feet high.
They descended the Wonadan glacier,
where they suffered terrible experiences.
The men were hungry and frozen and
were compelled TO slip and slide down
precipices, as they were wearing boots
without nails. They became lost among
the pinnacles and peaks.


One of the Hungarians fell into a
crevice and was killed. Another, who
was injured, managed to crawl into the
village of Bourg, from which place
twelve Alpineists and guides set out to
search for the other three men. One was
discovered half frozen, but no trace could
be found of the other two. These men
are believed to have lost their lives, but
the search for them Is continuing. The
Hungarians said that they had never
climbed mountains before. They de-
olared their only idea was to walk
northwards toward liberty.

Washington welcomed its 1ost bat

ing it today with enthusiasm and
heartfelt gratitude for its return after
vicissitudes and hardships and suffer
ings. The men Of the 312th Machine
Gun Battalion not only got into action
in France, but played very important
part in the allied advance last autumn
that broke the German strength. Their
service in the capture of Montfaucon
and their advance through the Argonne
marked them as men st that high quail
ity that made American participation
in the war the finally deciding factor.
They finched at nothing. In the Ar
gonne their work was of the most diff
cult kind, the most dangerous. It was
upon this terrain that the Germans
based their confident expectation of
ability to hold the general line. The
American advance through it astound-
ed them and broke their spirit. And
it was in this advance that the men
Of the 312th distinguished themselves,
suffering serious losses. Many of
those who went forth from here and
were enrolled in this unit now lie in
France. Others are crippled. Some
are recovering even now from their
wounds. For all of them, those who
have returned and those who have been
lost, the capital pays its highest trib-
ute of admiration and affection.

WATERBURY, Conn, June 19.-
Pitched battles occurred here tonight
lasting for nearly an hour, between
the police and the strikers of several
brass factories. Pickets interfering
with workers precipf,ated the riot.
The city guards, deputy sheriffs and all
police and reserves, reinforced by
World War veterans who volunteered,
are patrolling the streets of the Brook
lyn district. where most of the strikers
reside.


The riot call was sounded at $40
p. m. Twelve policemen were injured,
three seriously. Patrolman John Moore
is not expected to live. Firemen pour
ing several streams on the masses of
strikers were stoned. Three were seri-
ously hurt.


Machine Guns on Roofs
Machine guns are mounted on the
roofs of buildings in the section where
the rioting occurred Thirty four
strikers were arrested up to midnight
many of whom were women. One
woman is held at police Headquarters
charged with lncltlng the riot. PATROL
man Peter Rice was stabbed twice and
beaten over the head with his own
club which striker took away from
him.


The other police were beaten with
clubs and baseball bats and were
struck by large cobblestones and
chunks of coai. T'i.e police duelIed the
rioters, after nearly an hours fighting.


City Hall Fortified


Fearing for the safety of the pris-
oners at the hands of the public, so
great was the indignation, the police
placed machine gun at the entrance
of the City Hall and one in the rear
wing Of the City Hall, where the police
station is located. Nurses from the fac
tory's inhrmares volunteered to dress
the injuries of those who were ar
rested and who were in many cases
seriously injured.


Orders were issued when the rioting
started to close the saloons in the dis
trict. OF those arrested all were
either Lithuanians, Russians, Poles or
Italians.

deaden the sound of the charge, so that

disturbed Upstairs the detectives

vinced that they had been watched.

freight train was blown from the

ward with great severity during the

The Mexicans know these trails as
a New Yorker knows Broadway-or
better. There are certain broad,
open. well travelled trails which lead
back from the border to the little
Mexican settlements. Some of them
can be navigated by wagon Many
others are only fit for horse and bur-
70 use. The first travellers laid them
out by following the natural grades
of the country. No doubt many of
them are thousands Of years old.


Back Of them are innumerable short
cuts and hidden trails. They go up
almost wall-like hills. They wind
through the baked and burned Bad
Lands. They tunnel under the
branches of the mesquite. Those who
know them can find water, perhaps
once day. perhaps more often. Those
who do not would suffer torments
with the heat and the thorns and the
constant labor. The lone scout would
be in danger of ambush every second.
A company of cavalrymen would be
advertised like a circus parade. The
banditti they chase could spend half
their time playing cards and still get
away.

carefully organized strike, involving

The strikers, who demand M eight

One automobile was overturned in a
Glitch, and Walter Dewitt, superin-
tendent Of the packing department, was
attacked. He emerged with blackened
eyes and severe scalp injuries. Joseph
Richards, who was with Dewitt. also
was slightly hurt.


The strikers remained in full control
Of the situation until Sheriff Brokaw,
with twenty deputies. arrived and scat
tered the picket patrols posted on the
roads. Ten supposed leaders were
arrested. The rest of the strikers dis
appeared, and the plant, idle all day.
resumed operations when the skilled
members Of the night shift reported
for duty


"Bolsheviki," according TO officials of

strike and for the fact that the strikers
tried direct action" These radicals.
it was declared, insinuated themselves

organized the foreign element, COM
prising Russians and Poles.


". R. Seigle. vice-president Of the
company, said the laborers were receiv-
ing on straight time IS cents an hour,

much as so cents They worked ten

ROUSES POINT, N. Y, Nov. 10.--Ed-
ward, Prince of Wales, entered the
United States tonight and received his
first welcome to the Republic at this
little out-of-theway New York town.


He was greeted officially by Secre-
tary of State Lansing with bemed-
allied staff of admirals and generals
in attendance, and the famous band of
the ODD United States Infantry blaring
God Save the King" Unofficially, he
received far more boisterous well
come from the 1000 inhabitants of
Rouses Point, who had waited patiently
for hours in the bleak north wind to
cheer the nations guest.


The special train carrying the Young
Prince crossed the Canadian border
soon after o'clock and a few minutes
Later pulled into the station here. Sec
Rotary lansing's train had arrived an
hour previously and the Secretary and
his staff were stardingf on the plat
form when the youthful heir to Bri-
~ain's throne ran down the steps OF his
car with the eager ster of boy


$50 In Guard of Honor


His appearance was the signal for
the band to break into the strains of
the British national anthem. while the
$50 picked men OF the 63d, who formed
the guard Of honor, presented arms
The Princes arm snapped up in quick
salute and he remained standing thus
"a slim soldierly figure-until the
last strains of the music had died
10 the salute again as the band played
the opening bars of The Star
Spangled Banner"


There was 10 formality or speech
making in correction with the Princes
initial welcome. He shook hands in
turn with Secretary Lansing Major
General John Biddle, representing the
United States Army; Rear Admiral
Albert 7. Niblck, representing the
Charleton, OF the British Army, rep
resenting the British Embassy, and
then with the officers Of lesser rank
belonging to the various stats. The
Prince laughing. apologized for using
his left hand, explaining that his right
lad been done in" Canada.


Twelve Prettiest Girls


After introductions had ended, the
Prince inspected the guard of honor.
When he reached the end of the front
rank. surprise awaited him. Rouses
Point had selected its twelve prettiest
girls to hold aloft q canopy formed
of two great American and British
Tags sewed together.


ooh, must speak to the ladies after
ward" exclaimed the Prince. He COM
pleted his inspection and returned to
the flag holders, passing under the
canopy and shaking hands with each
IN turn.


The soldiers moved off as he Prince
climbed aboard his car again and the
crowd surged about the observation
platform, where he stood, smiling and
waving his hand in acknowledgements
of their cheers.


Then he had another surprise. 1t ap-
peared as if Rouses's Point had de-
cided with one mind that they were
going to obtain the distinguished visi-
tors autograph and had equipped
themselves with everything for that
purpose. from stub pencils and memo
randum books to cabinet portraits and
fountain pens.


The secret service men waved them
back desperately, but one enterprising
woman reached the steps of the car
and to her delight the laughing prince
bent down and wrote his name in her
book.


Just before the train departed on its
long run to Washington. man darted
out of the crowd and shouted:


Will you give me the honor Of shak-
ing hands with you? I'm s. Canadian.
wounded and gassed at Vimy"


The prince leaned over the rail and
shook him heartily by the hand and
The train was off.

Mrs. George W. Wightman, former
national champion, came into her own
again yesterday, when she defeated
Miss Eleanor Goss in two out of three
sets at the West Side Tennis Club at
Forest Hills, and thereby won the
metropolitan singles tennis champion
ship. The scores were 1-6, Cd, 6-2.
Despite the gloomy day large gal
lery was present to witness the match,
which was one of the best played in the
tournament. 1t was a case of youth
and brilliance versus experience and
steadiness, and the latter qualities won
out. The court was rather heavy and
slowed up the play of both contestants
somewhat. Speed, however, was by no
means eliminated from the contest;
rather the velocity of play was one oe
the outstanding features of the after
noon.


Miss Goss, by sharply driven ard
we'll placed shots to the back court,
kept Mrs. Wightman away from the net
and on the defensive for a considerable
part of the early stages of the match.
In fact, Mrs. Wightman was very much
off form until we'll into the second set,
when she suddenly rallied, and from
then on she played with clocklike pre-
cision and steadiness and missed very
few opportunities.


Winner Varies Attack


When finally in stride she varied her
attack and kept her youthful opponent
hopping all over the court From
lob she would quickly shift to light
ning-like drive down the side lines or
by an excellent backhand stroke turn
aside swift shot destined for the very
edge of the back line of the court


For more than half the distance Miss
Goss looked like the victor.


After losing the opening game, Miss
Goss, by brilliant play, aided measur-
ably by missed opportunities on the
part of Mrs. Wightman, ran through
ten straight games. She had captured
the first set in easy fashion, 81, and
was we'll on her way to the champion
ship with four straight wins in the
second set when Mrs. Wightman braced.
She volleyed and parried almost cv-
cry shot thereafter in the second set,
permitting Miss Goss little time to get
set, and quickly ran through six
straight games for a Cd victory. This
sudden stand and reversal of form was
a marvellous display of keen tennis.


Miss Goss on Defensive


Both returned to the court after a
brief rest, but it was quickly discerned
that Miss Goss was not quite the same
player. She seemed to have lost her
confidence and now played more eau
tiously, with the result that her driv-
ing lacked the fire with which she had
annexed many points. She was quickly
put on the defensive by Mrs. Wight
mans rushing attack and in this posi-
ton she stood small chance of winning.
On the other hand Mrs. Wightman,
who had appeared cool in the losing
stages, now set forth to quickly end the
strife and banged away with all the
recklessness of an easy winner. Miss
Goss in this set showed flashes of her
earlier form and managed to gather

court for heresy. There was no military
ground upon which they could condemn her,

Ultimately this was the fate she suffered

years later Paris was lost to Henry VI.


Eventually she was sentenced to death,
but this sentence, after many appeals and
many efforts to involve others in its impo-
stion, was suspended. Then Joan was led
back to prison after being prepared FOR the
stake.


This so aroused the Burgundians and the
English that they laid new trap for her
and placed mems clothing in her way. She
adopted male attire again, this time as a
protection from her jailers, and was cited
as "relapsed hereto" She was tried on

ma Canal.

San Francisco to Honolulu, Manila,
Vladivostok and thence to Nagasaki,
Guam. Honolulu and San Francisco.

out of Siberia they will come on these
craft, which have made an unusual
record in the transport service to and

make the trip from San Francisco to
Manila in fifteen days, thus improving

LONDON, March 22.-The first ac-
count of remarkable long distance
flight over the North Sea which was

days is now officially published. The

characterized by extremely unfavor-

as ranking as perhaps the most not
able flight of the kind ever undertaken.


The total length of the round trip
was ,2S5 air miles, and the time taken
was about forty and half hours.


The airship started from the Firth
of Forth, laying a straight course
toward Denmark. There was a north
west wind of fifteen to twenty miles
an hour and the night was dark, but
the airship was only mile from her
course when she passed the Dogger
Bank lighthouse. Then the wind in
creased and calcium flares were
dropped into the sea frequently to de-
termine the location.


i He diiSHlp 3 troubles began on the
return Journey The wind became
stronger and more tempestuous. At
midnight one engine became useless
and the ship was forced considerable
distance to leeward. The captain con-
templated landing in France, but
finally decided to hold on in the hope
the wind would abate. The wind abat-
ing somewhat, a Gland fall" was made
at North Forel. At this time the
gasolene supply was running low and
only one engine could be kept run
ming.


During the last stage of the voy-
age the wind was very violent and the
crew had the greatest difficulty in con-
trolling the ship. All suffered in
tenscly from seasickness, especially
pilots and coxwains.

over the sea. 1t was the longest non

BALTIMORE, Md, May 50.-Twenty
thousand Jewish citizens marched
through the streets last evening and
held big meeting at the Lyric The
ater. to protest against outrages and
massacres in Poland and other parts
of Europe. Resolutions declaring that
American Jews had fought for world
democracy and protesting against the
massacres were adopted and copies
sent to President Wilson and the
peace conference.


The marchers carried banners bear
ing the Inscriptions: I'VE fought for
liberty and democracy for all peo-
pies; shall we be deprived of it?"
Peace will soon return to the world,
but will there be peace for the Jews?'
1.-TWO thousand American Jews gave
their lives for world freedom; are the
Jews to be outraged" At the head of
the line was the announcement in big
letters, This is no parade" The
bands played Chopin's funeral march.
Every marcher carried an American
flag.


Four Poles were arrested for tear
ing an inscription from an automobile.
Other attempts were made to inter-
fere with the procession, but large
forces of police prevented any serious
disturbances.

LONDON. May S Correspondence of
the Associated Press) Nearly every
one in England has changed butchers
in the past few weeks, or is doing so
now. When strict rationing was in
force each householder was compelled
to register with one butcher and buy
all meat from him. People were stand
ing in line for the butchers supplies,
his hoppers were cleaned every day
before his customers could get what
they wanted, and he was irritated at
price and allotment.


The result was that when the gov
eminent decided householders could
register with another firm nearly
everybody did. They all calculated
they could not injure their position.
The consumer is no longer required to
give coupons for meat, butter and su-
gar The grocer and the butcher still
are rationed. however. and they deal
out to their customers about the same
amount delivered to them when cou-
pons were required. The supplies to
the retailers are rapidly being in
creased.

onstration.

calmness for both sides and a restora- :
tion of amicable feeling.

The case with the Allies was entirely

out around the periphery Of a vast
circle. At the beginning of the war the
British Isles, France and Belgium con-
stituted one Allied cluster in north
western Europe Serbia and Montenegro
constituting second group-were

The northern sea passage to Russia
through the Baltic was sealed by Ger

When Italy came into the war. in

fronts were partially linked up. But
Italy had been a belligerent hardly six
months when Serbia and Montenegro
were overrun by the Germans. For
more than two years thereafter the
only secure footing left to the Allies in
the Balkan peninsula was the intrenched
camp of Salonica. In Asia there were
minor Allied operating fronts in lower
Palestine, in Mesopotamia and in Ar
menia-all distinct and widely separated
from one another. German communica-
tions radiated from the centre of the
circle, within which the Teuton powers

WASHINGTON. Oct. 6.-The disturbance
that was central Sunday night over the upper
lake region passed rapidly eastward, and
Monday night its centre was over the Gulf
of st. Lawrence. It has been attended by
showers in practically all districts east Of
the Mississippi River. except on the south
Atlantic coast, but Monday night the weather
had cleared generally east of the Mississippi
River. Showers have fallen also in the west
Gulf states. New Mexico and Southern Utah.


The weather is cooler in the interior dis
tricts east of the Mississippi River and along
the northern border east of Montana. Cooler
weather continues over the south plateau and
south Rocky Mountain regions.


The outlook is for fair weather Tuesday
and Wednesday generally east of the Mssis-
sippi River. Temperature will be lower in
the Atlantic states, the Ohio Valley and the
region of the Great Lakes.

LONDON, July 25.-By continued con-
ferences with the leaders of the striking
Yorkshire miners Premier Lloyd George
finally has reached something like set
tlement which will put the men back
at work The whole Yorkshire out
break apparently was caused by si'nn's
mistake in addition made by Sir Auck-
land Geddes and his advisers in tho
Ministry of Labor.


The miners doing piece work in the
Yorkshire district discovered that when
their demand for shorter hours was
granted they would not make as much
in wages as they had been receiving.
Therefore they put in a claim OF lab
per cent. increase wherever their hours
were reduced 10 per cent


About this simple little matter OF q
sliding scale arose an incredible amount
of mathematics and as the matter pro-
ceeded the Government officials became
more and more deeply involved in sta
tistics of all kinds. All this was confus-
ing and finally resulted in an official or
der that piece workers should receive
only 10 per cent. increase in wages.


Yorkshire mine owners agreed with
their men and were ready to sign an
agreement to pay the difference between
10 per cent and 1913 per cent, but the
Coal Controllers order stopped negotias
tions and the strike followed. The public
now lays the blame for the whole affair
upon Sir Auckland Geddes, with good
deal of censure for the Government,
which failed completely to discover the
real cause of the trouble and the simple
remedy required until serious results
were threatened.

But where metal ships would founder and

Once, when sailors really earned the name,


twas fun to play with Death
As we trod the good old wooden decks,


with iron men for crew;
Til the steamers-more's the pity-came,


disdaining heavens breath,
Driving sailing men before them til they'd

Yes, we mixed commands with curses, while


the bucko mates of yore


Used their fists and iron Delaying pins on

proved it when ashore

Ah, the good old days back yonder, when a


man could hoist his sails


With the old Blue Peter Hying-destina-

And slip out into the briny with a crew as
hard as nails,
While the sheets strained at their halyards,

Ave, the good old days are over, leaving
stranded high and dry
All the relics of past decade, with yawn-
ing, open seams;
And they seem for but one purpose-that's
to bring to such as

save those within my dreams.

WASHINGTON. Oct. 30.-Pressure is high
over the Atlantic states. high and rising over
the Far Northwest and low over a wide belt
extending from the upper Miss sissipp Valley
southwark to Texas, in which belt there are
Two storm centers one over Minnesota and
the other over Southeast Colorado.


Clouds covered much of the country, and
during the last twcnty-four hours rain fell
generally east Of the Rocky Mountains, and
there were SHOWS in North Dakota. Wyoming
and Montana The weather has become
much warmer over the southern plains states
the great central valleys and the lake region.
and the weather remains warm in the South
west and Gulf states. Cold weather con-
tinues in Far Western districts.


The outlook is for cloudy. showery weather
over much of the country east of the Missis-
sippi River during the next thrty-six to
forty-eght hours.


The temperature will rise Friday in the
middle Atlantic and New England states.
and it will fall Friday night and Saturday
in the region of the Great Lakes and Satur-
day in the Ohio and lower Mississippi val
leys.

OF the upper lake region and in the central
and southern Rocky Mountain region Else
where throughout the country the weather
has been generally fair.

Punctuation marks were first en-
played by Aristophanes. the
famous Greek dFamatist. who lived
centuries before Christ. The sys-
tenn devised by him did not become
generally known. and soon fell into
complete oblivion. II was nearly
one thousand years before anyone
made a similar attempt. In the time
OF Charles the Great, two distin-
guished scholars. Alcuin and War
nefrid, again introduced punctua-
tion marks. but their signs also fell
into disuse. The present system OF
punctuation. as used in all modern
languages with Insignificant varia-
tions, was introduced in the first
half of the sixteenth century by the
Venetian printer. Aldus Manutius.
He is the real father Of the punctua-
tion marks-the period. comma,
colon. semicolon, exclamation, and
Interrogation marks, aposthFophe
and inverted commas. Printers
gradually adopted Aldus' system,
which dnally became established
throughout Europe.

marked improvement in the relations
between these classes during the dee
ads, and the improvement seems to be

il wise business policy.

thousands that usually congregate

eve will drink tonight the last bottle

his audience. Yet one man they raised

finished.


II could propose many things in this
last toast, but l will not. Here's looking
at you, gentlemen"

words which even the wings of that si-
lence seemed to be floating back into the
mists where they belonged.

it, turned and vanished through the still
open door. Something glittering had
dropped from his hand It's metallic clink
as it hit the floor was heard clearly
throughout the room.

January 20, 1919"

Reports from all the Southern re-
sorts-Palm Beach, Miami Belleair and
other famous places where society
gathers in the winter-indicate the
season which is just beginning there
will be the most brilliant of any in the
last three years. Most of the hotels
already are opened and filling up rap
idly. villas have been leased apart
ments taken and Households are being
made ready for gay parties. Colonel
Robert NJ. Thompson already has ar
rived at Palm Beach, and his his house
boat, Everglades, in Biscayne Bay.


Dates already have been fixed for
tennis and golf tournaments, and
motor boat regatta will be held on Bis
cayne Bay February II and Is, when,
will be military man9uvres by q full
tests and other feats of the air.


The tennis tournament Palm Peach
will begin February "a, and golf tourna-
ments soon will start. The proceeds
from all these affairs will be turned
over to the Red Cross


The trains going South are crowded,
and through service now established is
making travel much more comfortable.
Private cars again are being used, and
soon Palm Beach and the other places
will present the appearance of pre-war
days.


The nearby resorts, Lakewood and
Atlantic City, are filled with New York
ers, and there is much entertaining at
all the hotels, dancing again having
come into popular favor.

BALTIMORE, December 27-The
live poultry market remained un-
usually firm during the entire week
due to the holiday trade The de-
mand was very active and excep-
tionai prices prevailed. Receipts were
lighter by boats than have been known
to weather conditions and there being
but little poultry in that section Of
the country Travelled by the steamers.


Turkeys. both alive and dressed
were unusually strong all week, but
went off as the market closed today
the New Year trade chickens have
the call. This line advanced sharply
on Friday in anticipation of next
weeks business. In view of the pres
ent ice conditions many boats were
not able to make all of the wharves
and hence the full supply did not
reach market. Choice and fat ducks
and geese were in fairly good demand,
with no surplus.


With the holiday demand pretty
well supplied. the movement of eggs
was again light, and while the re-
ceipts were moderate they were equal
to the trade wants. The cold storage
market was more active.


The potato market rules firmer, re-
ceipts running moderate on all grades
OF stock, and the movement is better.
Some stock arriving showed frost and
had to be sold lower.


Native and nearby garden truck
found a firm market. Most all lines
were light in receipts and sold to
advantage when quality was good.


Arrivals of all lines of cattle were
light and the market was quiet but
firm for top grades. but of common
to ordinary stock the supply was
ample and of uncertain value.


Flour market was quiet on account
of the holidays but prices unchanged:
The grain market was strong until
yesterday and today. when it eased
Off High grades of wheat have COM
manded larger premiums than ever
over government prices.

NEW YORK. December 27.-Seven
former German ships now anchored
in New York harbor were formally
transferred today by the United
States Shipping Board to the British
ministry of shipping, in accordance
with the order signed by President
Wilson, No formal ceremony marked
the transfer. Skeleton British crews
were placed aboard the vessels and
the American flag was replaced by
the union jack.


The transferred ships are the Graf
Waldersee, Pretoria. Kaiserin Au-
guste Victoria Zeppelin. Mobile. Prinz
Friedrich Wilhelm and the Cap Fin
isterre. For the past eleven weeks
British seamen have been here, wait
ing to go aboard the vessels.


Although no official information was
obtainable, 1t is understood that the
ships will remain here about two
weeks loading cargo. and then go
to an English port. where they will
be completely overhauled

Five marines were decorated with

Myers, commandant of the camp, read
the orders and decorated the young
men in the presence of four thousand
cheering comrades Nine. Grouitch.
wife of the Serbian minister at Wash
ington, witnessed the ceremonies and
congratulated the gallant boys on
their services for the allies.


Deeds of Personal Valor.
Each of the recipients of the COW
leted French decoration had performed
deeds of personal valor. They had
rescued comrades under fire, had car
r1ed food and water to distressed
fighters across shell-swept zones and
were credited with many other deeds
later reported to Gen. Petain.


In his orders comforting the deco
rations Gen. Petain said the young
men had shown an utter disregard of
personal peril. apparently never for a
moment considering their own fate
while other lives were in danger.


1T gives me the greatest pleasure
in the world to be the medium through
which these nobly won decorations
shall be delivered" said Gen. Myers


The men decorated are Second Lieut..
Robert o. Williams Marine Gunner
William T. Nice, Corp. A. r. Open
heimer. and Privates Charles Mitchell
and Ernest J. Wiedman.


One hundred and sixty overseas men
were discharged and left for their
homes at midnight. They were given
a rousing farewell by their lusty COM
rades, who sang about, every marine
song that has been written since
America entered the war.

A further break in the ranks OF the
Paterson silk manufacturers, who are
standing out against the demands OF the
radical labor element for the immediate
introduction Of a forty-four hour week,
occurred yesterday wnen four mills
agreed to its establishment, without
waiting until October 10, when the new
schedule will become operative by agree
ment. The mills acceding to the de-
mands are the Beaumont Silk Company
the American Silk Company, the Law
renee Silk Company and the Abram
Abrash Company. They employ $50
weavers, who returned to work. In all
about 1900 operatives are now working
under the forty-four hour schedule. Be-
tween 1000 and 5000 are still idle.


The first violence during the present
strike came yesterday when an effort
was made to induce more dyers in the
Riverside section to quit work. Three
strikers were arrested, charged with un-
lawful picketing. and a fourth, charged
with throwing stones. Leaders of the
Amalgamated Textile Workers of Amer
lea, radical organization, said they
feared they would be unable to prevent
further disorder. They assert that $500
OF the 5000 dyers in Paterson are out.

thus welcome its own back from the
front. 1t is important that the men
who have gone over and survived the
fight should be made to feel that they
have represented 4 real vital spirit
on the part Of the American people


The cheers that sound for them are
not merely cheers of gladness that they
have escaped from danger, but glaaness
that their services have been effective
and that the American participation in
the war has made for world bettermeat.

LIMERICK, April % (by The Asso-
ciated Press The town of Limerick
was set laughing this afternoon over
the manner in which the strikers who
Monday afternoon attended hurting
contest across the river and in the
evening were refused permission to
return home over the Sarstield bridge
outwitted the military and got home.


Marching from the Glare end Of
the bridge to long pavement, they
boarded a train for Limerick. When
left the cars and tried to pass the
soldiers at the gate While the argu-
ment was proceeding the other pas
scngers, who had remained concealed
in the train, darted for other doors
and windows and scattered in every
direction. The guard was unable to
halt them, and they all soon were
home.


The strike leaders promise further
developments, but 1t is believed moth
ing will be done until the Irish labor
congress leaders arrive from London:
The time for their arrival is kept
secret.


The strikers had passed the night on
the bridge and resumed their demon
strations this morning. The soldiers
were still obdurate and would not per-
nit the strikers to cross.


Daybreak found wan and hollow
eyed crowd Of men and women shiver-
ing in the chilly weather. They were
taken to cottages on the Glare side of
the River Shannon and given breakfast
by friends and sympathizers. Some of
the older ones had been provided with
beds during the night on cottage floors
but most of the crowd passed the night
in the open.


The attitude of "passive resistance
was continued during the night by the
strikers. The military maintained a
strict guard with large forces of SEN
tries and the guns III the armored tank
were fully manned.

Uncle Sans little April fool joke on
Jersey rhore and Philadelphia COM
muters goes into effect to-day All per-
sons committing TO these points by the
Pennsylvania and Jersey Central rail-
roads must attach photographs OF them
selves to 100 trip apd $50 trip season
tickets and their 100 trip annual tickets
or the slips will be rejected by the col
lectors. After May the rule will apply
to fifty trip tickets also.


The new ruling, which compels every
Communication ticket holder to get his pic
ture taken and to attach to the ticket a
small copy Of the photograph, precisely
as the army and navy and other Govern
ment departments required photographs
attached to passes issued, affects many
thousands of persons who take cottages
and bungalows somewhere along the
pleasant Jersey shore In the summer
time. as we'll OF course as other thou
sands that make their year around
homes on that ocean fringe. During the
summer many thousands OF people spend
two or three months at the seashore and
use the season trip tickets instead of the
regular Communication tickets.


The season tickets are sold at reduced
rates and the monthly Communication
tickets are issued on sliding scale. the
cost for the first month being but triflc
lower than the regular fare. For this
reason most summer travellers use the
season tickets The fact that these can
be used throughout the season developed
a custom that the Railroad Administra-
ton desired to end. Some travellers sold
season tickets 10 friends.


The ruling was made to apply to the
Communication tickets between New York
and Philadelphia. which are sold at
about fourth of the regular rate. and
to season tickets to the Jersey shore
because there has been more complaint
regarding this practice from these lines
than from other roads. The New York
Central and New York, New Haven and
Hartford commuters are not asked as
yet to get their pictures taken.


The new ruling requires photograph
to be furnished at the time the ticket Ia
purchased. Photographs should be one
and a half inches square. Ticket pur-
chasers must supply their own photo
graphs. but ticket agents will give ad-
dresses OF photographers prepared to
take pictures quickly and at reasonable
prices.

New York, July 17.-The rains that

dry weather in the Carolinas recently,
and the market in consequence de-
veloped further weakness on the rains,

Texas crop reports.

all good investments to lay away.

They are more than police. They

For eighteen months now this al

ernor Smith last winter proposed to

sistently against the "extravagance"

corps applied these selfsame terms

Entirely outside politics, with
the statutes of New york State as
their only guide, the troopers have
made good. Confronted by THEN
record, the Chief Executive who had
proposed their abolition has fol
lowed the example set by the rura

porters of the riders.

tween his father, Colonel D. B. Cooper,
and Carmack in 1908, attracted country
wide attention, has been murdered here
under mysterious circumstances.


Cooper's body was taken from Rich
land Greek to-day, soon after his blood
stained automobile had been found on
q bridge near his home in the fashion
able Belle Meade Park action. The
skull had been crushed, but there were
evidences that a violent struggle had
taken place.


A coroner's inquest late to-day de-
veloped no clews to the murderer or
murderers, but the police are proceed
ing on the theory that Cooper was
Iured from his home by robbers. This
theory is based on evidence that

short time before he disappeared
Thursday night.

MOUNT CLEMENS, Mich, Aug. 15.-
The amount of costs that Henry Ford
may receive from "The Chicago
Tribune" in addition to the six cents
damages awarded him last night by a
jury which heard his libel suit against
the Chicago newspaper will not exceed
$50. Under Michigan law, where
nominal damages are awarded, not
more than $50 costs can be assessed
against the losing party


Alfred Lucking, senior counsel for
Mr.: Ford, said to-day little attention
had been given to the matter of costs
and that until he had looked up the
law covering the case he could not say
how much the plaintiff could expect to
receive.


Among other attorneys the opinion
was held that in cases where damages
awarded amount to less than $50, the
costs collectible may not exceed the
Judgment awarded. In this event, Mr.
Ford could demand only six cents costs
from "The Tribune"

They answered the summons, many

Many mills and manufacturing es-

break in a water main on Somerset
street below Amber.


The main is one of the most i'm
portant in the northeastern section of
the city, supplying many big industrial
plants as well as hundreds of homes.


The break occurred about 1 o'clock
this morning. Fire engine companies
and the patrol wagon from the Bel
grade and Clearfield streets police sta
ton were returning from a fire at the.
establishment of Edward Dawson, dye
works, Amber and Somerset streets,
when the water main burst.


There was rumble and n roar and
the streets were filed with water. Law
renee Harper, patrol driver, of the Bel
gtade and Clearfeld streets police sta
ton, had difficulty in getting the horses
from the rushing water.


The noise awakened the neighborhood,
and all rushed downstairs to find their
homes flooded. Police from the Bel
grade and Ccarlield streets station
guarded the streets and aided the fam
lilies. Men from the Water Bureau
shut off the water.


Among the mills closed are those of
JosepR Gubbins, waist manufacturer,
2124 East Somerset street.


The fire at the dye works of Edward
Dawson started in the bleachery. The
flames were discovered by watchman.
The damage was slight.

By the Associated Press.


ARCHANGEL, Tuesday. April l.
Repeated bolshevik attacks along the
front line and both the right and left
flank positions controlling Odozer-
skaia were repulsed today by allied
forces. The Americans, French, Brit
ish and Russians, who, either sepa-
rately or together, are holding posi-
tions throughout this territory, which
is little more than 100 miles south
of Archangel, have everywhere held
their lines intact.


Losses Demoralize Enemy.


The bolsheviki. in spite of their
heavy losses yesterday, attacked the
railroad front south of Odozerskaia
at 10 o'clock this morning, but they
failed. Allied forces east of Bolshoia
Ozera, where Americans, Russians and
British are fighting, were under at
tack all day yesterday at point about
fifteen miles west of OdoZerskaia. and
four separate assaults were made
there again early this morning. All
broke down under the allied fire. Ac
cording to bolshevik prisoners the
enemy is somewhat demoralized be-
cause of his heavy losses during the
past two days.


In the Seletzskoe sector. forty miles
east Of Odozerskaia, the allied ad
vanced posts were attacked by a
strong enemy patrol this morning.
but the bolsheviki were driven back
by machine gun fire. losing two killed
and a number wounded. Seletzskoe
protects the allied flank along the
Odozerskaia front and the right flank
of the allied river front positions.

station they were conducted inside the
palace to the Throne Room, where there

and Queen Helena chatted for few

earnestly with King Victor Emmanuel,
Premier Orlando and others. The mas
sive staircases were lined with the
young men of the Kings Household
Guard.

Villa Savoy, which is just outside the
walls of the city, standing in magni-
ficent park.

William ], Henderson. music critic of the

on The Orchestra and Its Instruments
before an audience that comfortably filled
the Shuhert Theatre. The lecture was the
second event of the four meetings of the
newly organized Philharmonic Society


Mr.. Henderson was introduced by the
president of the society, Mrs. Ernest Thomas
Toogood, and his address was thoroughly
practical He wisely omitted the vast
amount of historical data relative to the
origin and growth of the orchestra which
probably would only have resulted in con-

character of the instruments. Nine musi-

qualities OF the instruments in the various
registers. Those Illustrated were the violin.
viola. cello. flute. oboe, English horn. clars-
net. bassoon. horn trumpet and trombone.
The supplemental Instruments. such as the
contra -bassoon. bass clarinet and Others
were described and their chief characteristics
told.

general orchestration. telling what is meant
by balance. color and other terms. At the
end of the lecture solos were played by John
cello: Anton Horner French horn; Paul
Cailet, clarinet, and several others. The
program closed with three songs well sung
by Marie Langston-Stone. Mary Miller
Mount was the efficient accompanst

THAT twenty four-hole match which

the Overbrook Golf Club yesterday in

played in this country. Only one other
match has ever equaled that, and that
was in 1915. when Mrs. Clarence II.
Vanderbeck, of the Philadelphia Cricket
Club, defeated Miss Alexa Stirling, the
present national champion, on the
twenty second green in the semifinal
match of the national championship at
the Onwentsia Club near Chicago.


Remarkable Match


One of the pleasant features of the
match was that not single hole was
won on f1uke and that practically
every one of the twenty four holes was
decided on the green with putters. At
the end of the first nine holes the two
players were all square. By the time
the fifth tee was reached on the second
round Mrs. Suddards was three up.
Mrs. Disston won the fifth and sixth
and the seventh and eighth were halved.
Playing the eighteenth hole. Mrs. Sud
dards was dormie, but the hole went to
Mrs. Disston.


The first five extra holes were
halved and in every case both players
were on each of these five greens in
the same number, of strokes and each
took the same number of puts. Play
ing the twenty fourth hole, which is
the sixth at Overlook, both were home
in three shots. Neither had a very
hard putt, but the fckle dame of for
tune was with Mrs. Dsston and she
sank her putt, while Mrs. Suddards
just missed hers and the longest match

The Sun welcomes President VIII

imperative need of doing something

Of the United States from the grip of
the terrific cost of living.


For weeks THE SUN has been striv-
ing without assistance from the Ex-
ecutive Department of the Govern
ment to stir the officials to act for the
relief Of the suffering public. For
months those authorities watched the
appalling and unchecked rise In the
prices Of the necessaries of life with
out doing one single thing for the
relief Of the population.


In vain the people called for help.
In vain they sought for action. Bu-
reaucracy, high salaried, well housed,
abundantly fed, paid no heed to their
appeals. But now the President him.
self has heard the cry and has given
his promise that one man at least In
the Executive Department shall use all
the power and authority of his office
TO save the country from the dangers
which beset 1t. The people and THE
SUN have won notable recruit to
their cause.


Whatever the President does that
is impartial and wise and practicable
10 curb the greedy men and organiza-
lions will have THE SUNS loyal sup
port. and THE SUN will rejoice sim
cerely If day comes when 1t can say
to its readers that to President VIII
SON they owe their heartfelt thanks
for the reduction of the burdens
which now Cypress them.

vided with bicycles. These men sped
away On their machines followed by
bullets from the military mon and
policemen accompanying Lord French.

Washington took advantage of
the unusually good weather yester-
day by going out hunting for au-
tumn leaves and nuts. practically
every automobile and street car re-
turning to the city. being filled with
the golden-hued branches.


1t was an ideal day for hiking
and the cool snap in the air kept
the Sunday afternoon promenaders
on the move. The usual corner
loungers around Seventh street and
Pennsylvania avenue were nowhere
to be seen. the chilled air being too
much for the coatless gatherings.


Nut gathering did not prove very
profitable to the mixers so they con-
soled themselves by gathering large
quantities of tinted leaves with
which to decorate their homes
Some of the less considerate leaf
gatherers broke whole branches
from trees. not only running the ap-
pearance but also the lives of the
trees.


Hotel Hobbies were crowded in the
evening and the supper dances
were in full swing and evidently
very popular with Washington.
There is little doubt but that dane
ing will be washington's favorite
pastime this winter.

game Bulkley made some pretty shots
and kept Gould on the jump through
out. Lyle Mahan, last years cham

BOSTON, Oct l3.-Anxiety about
the British steamer Port Chalmers
which was reported on fire at sea Sat-
urday night was dispelled to-day when
radio message from the coast guard
cutter Acushnet said that the Port
Chalmers was not in any trouble, and
was proceeding with two other vessels
to the assistance Of the wooden steamer
Ammonoosic. The Ammonoosic, the
message said, was leaking fore and aft
and would be in danger Of sinking if
her pumps gave out. The naval COM
munications' office here ascribed the
report that the Port Chalmers was
burning to confusion of messages,
one of which said that she was sending
up rockets.


1t was believed here that the Acush-
net would keep on and endeavor to
assist the Ammonoosic, although the
exact location of the disabled vessel
was in doubt, three different positions
having been given in radio messages
that have reached the Navy Yard. The
last report said the Ammonoosc was
in latitude 39.11 north; longitude 6O.23
west. All the positions given were
said to be not more than twenty or
thirty miles from that of the Port
Chalmers.

To THE EDITOR OF THE SuN--SI: The
advocates OF great terminal markets for
the receipt and distribution Of the city's
daily food supply never consider or con-
suit with the men who now receive and
distribute that supply


Perhaps 100000 people are fed
daily In Greater New York and the ter
ritory within fifteen miles OF the exist
ing wholesale markets, and the men who
accomplish this enormous task with but
little waste are really worthy of serious
consideration.


To satisfy the exacting desires and
tastes of the New York public the whole
known world is drawn upon.


You will find in one store grapes from
Spain, oranges and lemons from Sicily
and California. caulihower from Oregon,
France and Long Island. alligator pears
from Cuba. pineapples from the Isle of
Pines, bananas from Jamaica and onions
from Bermuda and Spain.


To bring together the produce of the
world, to have sufficient and yet not too
much. requires intelligence far beyond
the average, and the men who accomplish
this are the best judges OF how many
terminal markets the city needs and
where best located.


One,hundred and twenty-five years ago
they selected the section where they are
now established. Later a branch for the
convenience of the local trade in Brook
Ign and for the disposal of Long Island
produce was established in the Walla-
bout. Still later the poultry and meat
people moved to the Gansevoort Market,
and for the receipt and distribution of
rougher produce the. Harlem and the
Westminster avenue markets were
brought into existence


To-day the trade is firmly established
with facilities for receipt. distribution
and storage. In the section of the city
bounded by vesey street, Canal street,
West street and West Broadway num-
Der of streets are piped for cold air and
many OF the buildings are fully equipped
with refrigerating appliances.


Here are located the butter and egg
people, the wholesale grocery people and
the wholesale produce people.


They are permanently located and
would not change no matter how many
terminal markets the city might estabs
lish at the instance Of lawyers. pro-
moters or parlor socialists.


OF the food consumed daily only az
per cent is perishable vegetables, berries
and fruit. OF this amount only small
part could be diverted to artihcially
created terminals. The more important
commission houses buy outright from
shippers In many instances and make
advances in many more Instances and
naturally control deliveries. Such de-
liveries could not be diverted except with
the consent of the commission merchant.
The articles of food which make up the
other 96H per cent. cannot be helped by
terminal markets no matter where To-
Gated. The packers have their own
methods of distribution from privately
owned markets: so have the milk people.


There can be no better place for poul-
try than the Gansevoort Market


Potatoes, apples, cabbage, turnips and
all the rougher fruits and vegetables are
now delivered In carload lots wherever
desired within free lighterage districts.


Salt water and fresh water fish have
each their terminal established by the
men who make their living out of the
business and who are interested In doing
business as efficiently and economically
as possible. Salt fish. canned goods. gro
ceries could not be. diverted to artificial
terminal markets.


Millions OF city money can be wasted.
terminals that will not be used can be
built, but all the city win have will be
the experience OF cities like Chicago and
Philadelphia with artihcially located
wholesale markets.


EDWARD p DOYLE,
President Receivers and Distributors AS

Europe today regarding the posi-.

row-May Day. Never in the his
tory OF organized labor has May Day

demonstrations by the working

screly stricken in all respects by

watching acutely for any evidences

out at the slightest sign OF Bolshevik
uprisings.

cialists have been extremely active

have declared a general holiday to-
morrow. Although in France the So
cialists are still indignant over the
acquittal OF Villain, who shot their

poison in the food of her luncheon

automobile mechanic. Mrs. Storrs
died in department store emergency
hospital Immediately after lunch.

her to come to lunch and discuss the
question of divorce for the Storrs.

of her guest, ordered the meal and,
according to the police. placed the
poison in fruit cocktail.

at the home of her uncle, James D.
Esary, president of the Island Trans
portation Company. Under persistent
questioning the police said she ad-
mitted placing the poison in Mrs.
Storrs's food.

WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, w. Va.
Aug. 16-Whte Sulphur Springs has
never known more successful August,
with both the Greenbrler and The
White packed to capacity and cottagers
harborlng many friends who have come
for the great social weeks of August.
The crowd has been so heavy that the
rest rooms in the bath establishment
have been converted into sleeping
quarters, and surrounding resorts have
cared for many motor parties unable
to receive accomm odations here. Co
tillons are being revived at the Old
White this season. and the horse show
cotillon Friday night was great sue
cess, over 800 people dancing in the
famous old ballroom and about that
many forming an interested gallery.


The horse show at The Meadows was
the chief attraction this last week, as
it always is, and receipts at the gate
showed the largest attendance in the
history of the show. Many motor par
ties came from Charleston. Hot
Springs, Old Sweet Springs and other
points across the mountains.


The Plaza cup offered for the horses
in the harness class, went to Mrs.
James B. Weir, of Charleston, whose
Golden Sceptre, shown in National
shows and at Madison Square
Garden, won several cups at this
shown Mrs. Thornton Lewis drove
for Mrs. Weir. Miss Marie J.
Leary, of Greenwich. Conn, rode
Zip, Dickson Brother entry.
in the jumping class, capturing the
James R. Thomas cup. On the second
day Miss Leary rode Greenbrier, the
oh hat hac
been ridden by woman in any of the
shows here, and captured the blue rib
bon in jumping class.


The most brilliant event of the two
days show was the riding of Miss Carol
P Smith on Cherokee, an Indian pony,
who was so spirited that it was almost
impossible to check him. On the third
jump Cherokee cleared five feet for
three foot jump and shook Miss Smith
SO she lost her stirrups. Before She
could regain them, Cherokee, with ears
pointed, broke for the fourth jump and
Miss Smith went over in perfect form.
The feat was rewarded with the Haw
ley Cup and amid loud cheers from
an admiring gallery.


Miss Haldeman Rides


Miss Isabel Haldeman, of Louisville,
who has ridden in the shows here for
several seasons. rode Mrs. Lawrence
Lewiss Palm Tree in jumping class,
coming in for the red ribbon, and Palm
Tree was awarded another ribbon in
the five gated saddle class when Miss
Kenilworth added blue ribbon to his
long list. Moonshine, Dickson
Brothers entry, captured the hearts
of the gallery when he cleared high
jumps over six feet.


Rates Mountain Club was the scene
of two merry parties this week. Sun
day evening the Old Virginia dinner
was featured, and almost one hundred
people were present. Monday evening
by Colonel and Mrs. James r. Branch,

eral hundred members of the colony.

clair, of New York, gave a small tea

Ten thousand members and friends
OF the New York A. G.. journeyed BY
train, auto and yacht to Travers Island,
the beautiful summer home OF the Mer-
curry Footers, yesterday to see the an
nual spring meet, the 1920 games OF
Americas greatest athletic club.


The same setting as of yore was there.
The big oval. bordered by the cinder-
path upon which so much athletic his
tory has been made, shimmered under
the blazing sun. At one end stood the
sturdy elm whose massive boughs for
quarter of a century have sheltered
almost every track champion worth tell
ing about. At the other end blared the
band. The emerald terraces and banks
slipping up from the track were crowded
with spectators. the fair sex almost
outnumbering their escorts and with all
the colors that go with their summer
fnery making the terraces look like
fields of variegated peoples swaying in
the wind. Pretty girls as usual seemed
thicker than leaves In Vallombrosa.


But the record wrecking stunts, the
invariably fast times, herculean heayes
and wonderful leaps that writ so
many Mercury Foot carnivals into ath-
letic history, were missing. Competition.
1t Ia true, was keen and exciting, but
the performances were mediocre and at
no stage was Father Time endangered
Not once during the afternoon did some
famous champion come racing up from
the rear. knitting his way with long
bounding strides through the field to
tear the tape victor. Race after race
was reeled off without a back marker
showing to the fore. Laurels almost in
variably went to the ones up front with
the long handicaps.

LONDON, May 3.--Residents Of the
West End of London turned out in
force to-day to welcome 1900 over
seas troops who marched through the
main streets and were reviewed by
King George at Buckingham Palace.
Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South
Africa and Newfoundland were repre-
sented.


Among the guests of King George
on the reviewing stand were Josephus
Daniels, American Secretary of the
Navy, and his staff. Every arm of the
overseas armies was represented in
the parade, while famous Canadian
airmen flew overhead.


General Currie of the Canadian
army, with his staff, including Prince
Arthur of Connaught, headed the pro-
cession. Each unit was headed by
commanding officers and their staffs.
The parade was one of the many dem
onstrations designed to announce the
coming of peace.

The commander at Compicgne, evidently
in panic as the noise of the fighting drew
nearer raised the drawbridgc Joan and
many of those with her in the sortie were
left outside. She was taken prisoner


Joan was held captive for many months.
No effort was made by the King to ex.
change or ransom her. In the mean time
she was a problem to her captors. They
could only cite her before an ecclesiastical
court for heresy. There was no military
ground upon which they could condemn her,
for she had merely beaten them.


Ultimately this was the fate she suffered
and there has been much written upon the
subject of her trial and its legality.


She faced her accusers fearlessly and re-
sisted all efforts to confuse her. On March
1 Joan stated that "within seven years
space the English would have to forfeit a
bigger prize than Orleans" Less than seven
years later Paris was lost to Henry VI.


Eventually she was sentenced to death,
but this sentence, after many appeals and
many efforts to involve others in its impo-
stion, was suspended. Then Joan was led
back to prison after being prepared FOR the
stake.


This so aroused the Burgundians and the
English that they laid new trap for her
and placed mems clothing in her way. She
adopted male attire again, this time as a
protection from her jailers, and was cited
as "relapsed hereto" She was tried on
May 81, 1881, and the sentence was carried
out the next day

BERLIN, Monday, April % (By The
Associated Press Mot content with
just having survived three consecutive
Easter holidays, with three more holi-
days to come at the end Of May, the
workers Of Berlin and Germany gem
orally will rest from their excessive
labor on May /. the latest and new
est Socialist holiday in this country.


All transportation will be suspended
on the Berlin street cars, the suburban
trains and subways. Long distance
train service will be limited to food
and milk trains. Not even coal ship
ments will move.


Almost the only workers on May
Day will be the postmcn and post
women, who will carry out the Sunday
schedule of deliveries. and the tele-
phone operators, who will continue to
inflict their exasperating service on
the public, which, though Of the long
suffering kind, has been protesting in
increasing measure the past month.


The theatres will be closed, and
even the restaurants will shut down
unless the swelling protest Of the
thousands who depend upon public
eating places is needed. 1t is proposed
that such restaurant employees as can
cook, serve food and clean dishes shall
work at least part Of the day in res
taurants where food, rather than
drink forms the major portion Of the


business.

Two boys, each twelve years old,

street above Cambria, and William Gil

Westmoreland streets station, said that
on Sunday afternoon the pair forced a
window at the Office of the Philadelphia
Electric Company, Kensington avenue
and Westmoreland street. They at
tackled the safe with a hammer and
chisel, but were unable to open it, he
said. They took revolver and So
in cash from drawer in the Office,
according to the detective.


Later in the day the boys entered the
coal Office of Magee Brothers, Ontario
avenue and G street, where they broke
open the safe and stole $40 in cash and
number of Liberty Bonds, the detec-
tive says. n'

fessed. They will have a hearing today

And saw the westward going stars


Pass slowly out of sight.
Slowly the bright procession


Went down the cleaning arch,
And my soul discerned the music


Of their long triumphal march.
Till the great celestial army,


Stretching far beyond the poles,
Became the eternal symbol


OF the mighty march of souls.
Onward, forever onward,


Red Mars led down his clan;
And the moon, like a mailed maiden,


Was riding in the van.
And some were bright in beauty, =.


And some were faint and small,
But these might be in their great height


The noblest OF them all.
Downward, forever downward,


Behind. Earth's dusky shore
They passed into the unknown night,


They passed and were no more.
No more! Oh, say not so!


And downward is not just;
For the sight is weak and the sense is dim


That looks through heated dust.
And though the hills of Death


May hide the bright array,
The marshaled brotherhood of souls.


Still keeps its upward way
And long let me remember,
That the palest faintest one
May to the diviner vision be
A bright and blazing sun.
Thomas Buchanan Read

negrins. asserted ethnographic, histor-

Six frightened children were helped
from the house at 3OS Kimball street
when it caught fire early today.

of the children, works to support them.
She left the house early this morning

thought that a candle was burning on
the mantel in the front room when she
departed, and that the candle, burning
down, fell from the mantei to the bed
on which the children slept. The bed
was soon in flames.


Patrolman Lerner, of the Seventh and
Carpenter streets station, saw smoke
issuing from a window. He helped the
children to the street and called the
fire department. The blaze was soon
put out.


The rescued children were Ida, fifteen
years old; Lillian, fourteen; Anna.
eleven: Fannie, nine; Louis, six, and

some action toward restocking the river
with young fish. the shad will disap-
pear entirely from the waters. They
assert further that the sewerage and
pollution of the river is driving the
shad from their old haunts into clearer
waters.


They point out that not enough fish
!, have been caught this year between
Philadelphia and the Breakwater to
provide sufficient spawn to keep the
hatchery at Torresdale busy. and say
spawn will have to be obtained from
southern waters.


Fishermen are powerless to supply
the increased demand for shad, which
Is now up to So per plate at Jersey
planked shad dinner hotels. Fishermen
operating nets at Camden, Gloucester,
Billingsport and other nearby places
said today that the run of shad this
season is the poorest they have ever
known.

enough to meet expenses or to supply
demand. The fish are bringing high
prices and no roe shad can be obtained

cester, said today he has not caught a

TRENTON. NJ, May 1.-Two Italian
prisoners at the New Jersey state
prison late this afternoon prevented
the Escape from that institution of
three murderers and one prisoner serv-
ing thirty years for intent to kill The
Italians, whose names are withheld by
Principal Keeper Mulheron. will be
recommended to the Pardons Board for
paroles.


The men who nearly gained their
freedom were Charles Evans. of Essex
County, who murdered policeman
and citizen; Robert Sheridan, of Hud-
son County. convicted Of assault with
intent to kill; George Gardner, of Som
erset County, serving from twenty to
thirty years for murder, and Raymo ond
Fisher, of Hudson County, convicted Of
murder in the second degree. Gardner.
with Richard Hammock, killed motor
truck driver near Bound Brook some
months ago.


The prisoners, while at work in the
shops, managed to make a rope ladder
to which they fastened large hooks.
Secreting the ladder beneath some rub
blsh they were instructed to carry from
the prison to tho yards, they threw the
ladder and the hooks caught on the
top Of the prison wall.


In twinkling the men were scram-
bling up the wall, and were just about
to step to freedom when the Italians,
serving sentences for trivial offences,
saw them and pulled the ladder down.
Enraged at the interference with their
escape, the four men pounced upon the
Italians and nearly beat them into in
sensibility. The cries of the Italians
were heard by James Shea, a tower
guard, who drew his gun and sounded a
general alarm. The four man were
soon handcuffed and placed in cells.
