MARIA, Tex, Aug. 20.-The Amer
lean punitive expedition that raced
into Mexico in search of Jesus Rem
teria's band of bandits who held
Lieutenants Peterson and Davis for
ransom, went to camp in the noun
tains tonight after trying thirty-si
hours of campaigning through rugged
country.


Since the troops crossed the Rio
Grande early Monday morning they
have been riding constantly during
daylight hours.


The only reported contact with the
bandits resulted in the killing of one
of three Mexicans who fired on an
American airplane yesterday. Accord
ing to the aviator's report upon re-
turning from the field, the fight lasted
twenty minutes. The aviators were
unharmed.


The American troops have progressed
so far into the interior of Mexico that 1t
has been found impracticable to get
forage and heavy materials over the
trails. To-day the cavalry obtained feed
for the horses from natives paying cash
for all purchases. Long wagon trains
arcs plying between the Quartermaster
depots here and the field base on the
Rio Grande, carrying rations and sup
plies for the troops of the punitive expe-
dition


The soldiers are spending their second
night under Mexican skies under more
favorable conditions than last night.
There has been rain since yesterday and
the ground dries rapidly in the Mexican
desert country.


A cryptic message, "Stiii following
tIail,9 brought to the border by airplane
to-day, was the only definite word from
the expedition. No officers commanding
uoops in the field have yet returned to
the field bases on the river.


Major-Gen. Joseph T Dickman, Com
roander of the Southern Department. is
expected to reach here tomorrow morn
ing.


Reports from Preside, Tex, told of
movements of Mexican Federal cavalry
under Gen. Antonio Pruneda to-day.
Gen. Pruneda left OJinaga last night,
marching toward Cuchillo Parade. forty
fliles up the Conchos River.

KEY WEST, Fla. September IL
With daylight today, following the
storm of yesterday, and a night of
darkness, the people Of Key West and
surrounding territory were able for
the first time to survey the destruc-
ton wrought by the hurricane that
swept through here Tuesday night.
Not house in the city had escaped
damage and many were totally
wrecked.


Conservative estimates place the
property loss at not less than two mill
lion dollars. The federal building was
badly damaged. The harbor presented
a tangled mass of fishing vessels and
other small craft, but latest reports
on the dredge Grampus. OF the four
teen men on this craft ten were res
cued last night, one body was recov-
cred and three are missing. The Brit
ish tanker Tonawanda, which had to
be scuttled to save the liner Comal
after that vessel had broken her moor
ings and gone aground, was reported
not in a bad position. The steamer
st. Gougal also broke loose.


Traffic Is ParalyZed.


No vessels had left port early day.
nor had any trains come in over the
Florida East Coast railway. In adj
dition to the temporary stoppage of
gas and electricity, the telephone serv-
ice was suspended and newspapers
were forced to suspend publication.


Some business places, all of which
were closed yesterday. including res
taurants, reopened today. A survey
today of the situation resulting from
the storm was expected to determine
whether it would be necessary to ask
outside assistance.


Forty-Five Reported Adrift.


MIAMI, Fla, September ia
wireless message received here early
this morning said forty-five persons
were adrift in small boats between
Fowey Rock lighthouse and Cape
Florida, about fifteen miles from Mi
ami. All were reported Gin distress
and without food or water. No de-
tails were given and there was moth
ing to indicate their identity, but it
was presumed they were members of
crews of ships that went down dur
ing the hurricane that swept this
section early yesterday. Boats have
left here to bring them in.

Thieves stole $1,000 worth of clothing,
silver, table linens and fine liquors from
the home of Mrs. David Lewis, &c South
Twenty second street, while the house
was closed during Major David Lewis's
absence in the army.


The theft was discovered by Mrs.
Lewis Thursday, when she went to her
home to show a friend through It,.
While Major Lewis was away the house
was closed and Mrs. Lewis was living
at the Lincoln Apartments, Thirteenth
and Locust streets. Major Lewis has
just returned from the service in the
army


So far no arrests have been made The
theft was reported to the police late
Thursday. Mrs. Lewis waited several
hours after discovering it in an effort to
get in touch with her husband before
she called in the police.


The thieves left the house in state
of great confusion. They evidently took
their time about the robbery; going into
every room. and searching every possible
hiding place for valuabes.
Mrs. Lewis found the contents of
bureau drawers scattered over the floors
of the bedrooms trunks forced open
and clothing strewn everywhere; even a
phonograph smashed in the search for
valuables.


Among the articles taken were a
number of pieces of Sheffield silver, Mrs.
Lewis's whole collection. Other large
and small pieces of silverware were
stolen.


Two overcoats, three suits of clothes
and half a dozen pairs of shoes were
carried off by the thieves. From the
linen closet they took fine table linen,
tablecloths and napkins. The wine
closet was broken open and a quantity
| of fine liquors taken.


, There was nothing to indicate when
| the theft took place. Apparently the
| thieves had forced their way into the
house by prying open a shutter in the
back Kitchen.

BALTIMORE, November 4.-One of
the most daring hold-ups in Cecil
county was perpetrated last night
when forty men were. held up and
robbed in house on the state road
between Port Deposit and Liberty
Grove by four Italians at pistol point.


The men charged with 1.-The crime
were arrested later and lodged in the
Elkton jail. They gave their names
and addresses as John Toll. PIT Perry
street. Baltimore; Nick CARLY, Febas-
dry Descio and Sazerio Terra, the
three latter Of Philadelphia.


The men held up comprised party
that is working on the state road.
They were in their house about 8
o'clock, when the four men entered.


Covering the forty men with revol-
vers three of the strangers ordered
the men to hold up their hands. The
fourth man. with razor. went along
the line and slashed open the trouser
pockets of the forty, taking $500. They
then made their escape.


Later four men were arrested at
Port Deposit, while trying to get to
the Pennsylvania railroad tracks, and
taken back to Elkton. The money
was found In the shoes of some, while
others had money in their hatbands.

CHICAGO, Jan. 81. - The United
States has been made by the war a
centre of the diamond cutting trade.
Formerly Amsterdam and Antwerp
were the principal diamond markets
of the world. sIn those cities diamond
cutting and polishing have flourished
from the fifteenth century, when the
art of cutting diamonds was first
learned. All the great crown diamonds
of Europe, including the Kohinoor
and the Cullinan diamonds, the most
famous gems in the crown of England,
have been cut or recut by the experts
of these cities.


Now there are thrty-six diamond
cutting establishments in the United
States. mostly in New York. employ
ing more than 500 cutters, who make
from $50 to $75 a week. The United
States has become in recent years the
largest diamond importing and dia-
mond wearing nation on the globe
More than half-nearIy two thirds-
of the diamonds imported into this
country now are rough diamonds and
are cut here. 1t has been estimated
that more than half the diamonds in
the world are now owned in the United
States.


Whether this is correct or not, the
United States during the war bought
85 per cent Of the output of the South
African mines, which are now virtually
the worlds only source of supply

Joseph Cohen Of Rockaway Park and
Harry Norman of 10 Clinton street were
shot from behind yesterday afternoon
while they were walking on the west
side Of West Twenty-second street,
Coney Island. Cohen was struck be-
hind the shoulder blade. the bullet pene-
trating his lung and killing him almost
instantly. Norman was hit three times
in the back and side and was taken to
the Coney Island Hospital. where II
wac said by physicians that he would
recover. The police say that a third
man. Max Barron. was with Norman
the slayer and ran. SO far the police
have been unable to ind him.


Acting Captain of Detectives John Nc

District Attorney, began an investiga-
ton OF the shooting, and some hours
later detectives were sent to the hospital
and placed Norman under arrest on
charge OF homicide. This action was
taken after Mr.. Wilson had talked to
Emmanuel Cohen, brother of Joseph
Cohen. who declared that the shooting
was the outcome of business rivalry be-
tween Cohen and Norman and Barron.
Emmanuel Cohen also told the Assistant
District Attorney that Barron was I'M
der indictment for extorting $1,000 from

pending in General Sessions The detec-
tives have been unable to find any one
who saw the shooting. West Twenty

Norman told detectives who talked to

but that he believed the shooting was

and a piano player named Sam were
concerned.

they quarreled again.


The row was terminated by the piano
player and the woman jumping into the
touring car and leaving. saying they
were going to return to Manhattan.
Norman and Barron then telephone1
Cohen. a mutual friend. who operates a
straw hat factory In TOT Broadway. a
furrier's place in 673 Broadway. and
lives In % North Beach street. Rock
way Park, and after a few hours
Cohen Joined them at the island.
Then. Norman said. the three Of them
went hunting for a stranger who had

In the Coney Island place. They walkeu
through West Twenty-second street. in.

LONDON, June 2S.-London learned
peace treaty at Versailles. The news
became known through the firing of
runs which had been installed during
he war to warn the city of air raids.
These guns now were used as harbin-
gers of the long awaited peace.


The moving throngs came to halt
when the first report was heard. The
tension lasted but few seconds. Then
the people gave themselves up to cele-
bration of the event.


After news of the signing of peace
had been officially received, the follow
ing was issued over King Georges sig
nature:


"The signing of the treaty Of
peace will be received with deep
thankfulness throughout the British
Empire. This formal act brings to
its concluding stages the terrible war
which has devastated Europe and dis
tracted the world. 1t manifests the "
victory of ideals, of freedom and of
liberty for which we have made un-
told sacrifices.


81 share my peoples joy and
thanksgiving, and earnestly pray that
coming years of peace may bring to
them every increasing happiness and
prosperity. GEORGE K. l."

Flag sellers all over the city did a
brisk trade. Their wares were bought
Eagerly and were thrown to the breeze
by the cheering thousands.


The great bells of St. Paul's Cathe-
dral and Westminster Abbey, and virtu-
ally all the churches of the metropo-
lis, added to the din. Bands of Boy
in, tba,

bugles and the beating of drums.

was magnet that drew many other
thousands. The crowds poured into the
square, cheering as they came. White
hall and other centres, including Hyde
Park, also had their demonstrations.

Thousands of Boy Scouts, drawn by
the blowing of many whistles, gathered
to celebrate in Hyde Park In fact the
whole West End suburban district par
ticipated in the celebration. The only
quiet spot was the square mile which
composes the City of London proper,
and which is always deserted Satur-
day afternoons. Even there flags were
soon flying.


In theatres and other places of
amusement the news was communicated
imme diately to the audiences. The peo-
pie rose and cheered and sang the ma
tional anthem. Newsboys soon came
with special editions. They carried the
hugs posters, customarly issued by
newspapers here, and these gave the
people all the news they wanted for
She moment. The posters read: peace

bled before Buckingham Palace. King
George, Queen Mary and other mem
hers of the royal family appeared on
the balcony. The Guards band played
national airs and the crowd sang. The
vast mass of people was constantly
changing, newcomers replacing those
who left. Members Of the royal
family, after leaving the balcony, rs-

Lieutenant Colonel John B. Carnctt
commander of Base Hospital Unit No.
90 the University of Pennsylvania unit,
is home on furlough.


Ten other surgeons attached to the
unit also are home. All will have to
return to Camp Dix early this week
for demobilization. They arrived in
Boston aboard the Patricia on Friday
night, and were sent to Camp Devens,
Aver, Mass.


The Carnett home at 123 South Twcn-
tieth street, is a happy place, with the
colonel telling everything about every
body's experiences with the unit but
his own. And his were most heroic.


Organizer of the unit and chief means
of collecting the 500, 600 raised to en-
dow it, Colonel Carnett did not COM
mand it when it went overseas in April
of last year. A regular army man got
that job.


But while sthe main unit remained at
Chateau Guyon, where it did great
work, Colonel Carnett headed mobile
unit that followed the American army
in all its great drives, land the team
was in the thick of the fighting and
+, hard work through which the army
passed.


Lorraine, Chateau Thierry, st.
Mihiel and the Argonne-thcy are all
more than mere names to the members
of the mobile team.


They experienced them. Under com
mand Of the colonel they were right
behind and with the fighting units ut
all times and exposed TO all the dangers
of the enemy artillery fire. General
Pershing cited the team for its cool
ness under fire when its hospital shack
was shelled at Busy lie Chateau.


Those in the team were George NJ.
Laws, Captain Nathan Goldsmith,
Miss Helen Pratt, Miss Mary Berg
stresser, Bert" Bell, the university
football star, and Rufus Jones. r


Colonel Carnett has the highest
praise for the enlisted personnel and
officers of the entire hospital unit and
cited case after case where the cool
ncss and ability of the surgeons and
cooperation of the nurses and men had
resulted in victory over death on the
operation table.


Colonel Carnett took over the com
mand of his favorite unit after the
Argopne drive.

VINO rest in England gave their lives
in the same cause and their remains
represent the same salvation as those
who lie on the battledelds.

stitute if they are allowed to remain,
a perpetual reminder to our allies of
the liberty and ideals upon which the
greatness of America rests. | think
these sentiments are held by many
who have given this subject thought.

relatives and friends. | recommend
that none of our dead be removed from

Pacific Fleet OF the United States Navy
steamed into Colon at dawn to-day. The
warships after taking on oil and coal
went through Gatun Locks. the first
stage in the Panama Canal journey from
the Atlantic to the Pacific. this after
noon.


Airplanes escorted the fleet into the
harbor where great crowds lined the
shores for a sight of the dreadnoughtA


The fleet movement so far has pro-
ceeded without a hitch. The battleships
Georgia and Vermont Joined the feet
here to-day.


Some time tonight II is expected the
feet will reach Gatun Lake and anchor
there until sunrise when the journey
will be resumed until Balboa, at the
Pacific end of the canal, is reached. The
fleet will remain there until Monday.


Welcoming receptions and entertain
ments of various kinds have been ar
ranged.


Admiral Hugh Rodman. commanding
the feet. took the bridge on his flagship.
the New Mexico, at sunrise to-day and
directed the passage of the warships
through the Colon breakwater to the
docks, where the New Mexico and the
Mississippi began taking on oil and the
New York and Wyoming coal. Mean
while the battleships Arkansas and
Texas proceeded to Gatun Lake where
they took on coal from barges.

GREEN RIVER, wyo., Aug. 10
Making a record run Of seventy-six
miles, the Motor Transport Corps
transcontinental train reached Green
River late yesterday afternoon without
operating or mechanical troubles OF
Importance to report.


There were a few miles OF good.
graded, dirt road, but during most of
the day the convoy followed deeply
rutted wheel paths along natural con-
tours with many holes and washouts.


A fifty-mile wind chilled the men
and raised clouds OF penetrating dust.
Twice the train ran into dust storms
of unusual severity, which obscured
vision entirely.


For twenty-five miles the way led
through passes and canyons with solid
sides rising 700 feet on each hand
fantastic in color and in line. The re-
mainder OF the run was through dry
parched country. entirely devoid OF
vegetation and trees, and strewn with
bones Of animals. The convoy camped
last night at the fair grounds, on the
banks of the Green river. Tomorrow's
run will take the train to Fort
Bridger.

Frank Reilly, thirty years old, 24O6

early this morning at Fifteenth street
and Columbia avenue by 4 plain clothes
patrolman. during brawl among ten
men and women.


The killing occurred few yards
from the tailor shop of Robert Stuart,
where thieves recently stole $4,000
worth Of cloth.


Reilly, according to the police, was
one of a crowd Of men and women who
began quarreling in a restaurant at
1892 Columbia avenue. The proprietor
succeeded in ejecting the brawlers. The
fight was continued On the sidewalk.


Patrclman Pagan, of the Nineteenth
and oxford streets station, was on plain
clothes duty in the neighborhood. He
had been assigned to that duty after the
Stuart robbery Pagan and another
brawlers and tried to quell the disorder

police assert, turned on the two police
men and were beating them when Pagan
drew his revolver and fired. The bullet
struck Reilly, killing him instantly.


The body was taken to ST. Joseph 3
Hospital, where the man was pronounced
dead. Pagan was held without bail by
Magistrate Grelis, to await action by the
Coroner.


Most of the crowd ran after the shoot
ing, but several arrests were made.

and with the same feeling of appre-

Alderman Quinn's assertion that
Mayor Hylan and Richard E. Enrght,

Cumberland. Md, Sept. 2.-The Bal
timore and Ohio Railroad shopmen went
on strike here this morning. having
voted to reject President Wilson's plan
Of settlement. The men numbered about
1900. The entire shop system is vir-
tually at standstil. The men who
struck include machinists, machinists'
helpers bolermakers, bolermakers'
helpers. sheet metalworkers, electrical
workers. blacksmiths and all foremen
from the general foreman down.


The car knockers. car repairers and
ripp traCkmen have also struck. Only
a few laborers are at work.


The Baltimore and Ohio men made
an unusually large showing in the Labor
Day parade yesterday and their de-
meanor portended the action of today.
All through their ranks were carried
banners calling for the adoption of the
Plumb plan and inveighing against
'capitalistic control" A number of
the older heads among the machinists
are said to have counseled against strik-
ing. but were overruled by the younger
element.

London. July 19.-Great Britain's
celebration of peace officially culmi-

hour It had not even abated.

parks, the cafes and the theaters.

gayety more typical of Paris than
London. There was every indication
that tens Of thousands would still be
celebrating at dawn.


Demonstrations were held through
out the empire. but the greatest in
terest centered in the parade here.
Nineteen thousand allied veterans, rep
resenting twelve nations, marched
through the heart of the city between
lines of wildly enthusiastic civilians.
Their ranks extended for, six miles
and half.


With Gen Pershing at their head
a composite regiment of $500 Amer
leans led the procession. Field
Marshal Haig headed the British
forces. Others in line included
French. Italians. Belgians and de-
tachments from Serbia, Rumania,
Portugal. Japan. Poland, Czecho-
slovakia, Greece. China and Siam.

Honolulu. T. H., Sept 30.-(By
A. P.)-Mount Mauna Loa, on Hilo
Island, burst into new eruption late
last night and a wide stream of lava
began pouring down the Kona side,
destroying many homes.


The residents of the Kona side are
reported fleeing TO the sea, which is
thirty miles distant.


The mountain, which is 10000 feet
high, first became active three days
ago, when smoke and gases came from
the crater. During the last two days
the eruption had been subsiding until
late last night, when the lava began
pouring down the Kona side.


Mauna Loa has been intermittently
active for many years, the most recent
outbreak having been in 1916, when
streams of lava poured down the west
ern side and steam and smoke
rose 10000 feet into the air. Seven
years before that, the lava outrush
carried nearly to Hilo. The crater of
Mauna Loa is 1900 feet above the
ocean, and II, 900 feet across. Kilauea,
the. fire lake, or crater, is easily acces
sible and an auto can be driven nearly
to the edge. Tradition says that Ruth,
who governed the islands, controlled the
volcano in 1881 by throwing a live pig,
plug of tobacco and a bottle of gin
into the crater

armies from the end of April, 1918,
when the situation was most critical,
up to the conclusion of the armstice.

of the situation when the British ar
mics had been forced to give ground be-
fore the tremendous German onslaught
in the spring offensive and when the
German forces on the Western front
greatly outnumbered those of the Allies.

ie-Francoise she was wounded in the

work with the wounded poilus, and
was taken prisoner near Malincourt,
after having been wounded in the
thigh. She was placed in a prison
camp in Alsace-Lorraine, and Ger
man major, learning that she was a
French nurse, attempted to attack her.

the arteries of her wrists, and was
transferred to hospital for treat
ment. After eight months in the hos
pital, she determined to escape, and
one night chloroformed twenty-five
wounded Germans who were in the
same room with her and left the hos
pital. Crawling from she'll hole to
shell hole, she made her way to the
French line.


Mile. Gauthicr was wounded twice
after her escape, and for weeks how
cred between life and death. Her par
ents were killed by German bomb
dropped by Hun aviator. and her
only brother, a soldier in the French
army, died in her arms. Later. for a
year and half, she served with the
American forces.


The French government gave Mile.
Gauthier the Cross of the Legion Of
Honor, the Medaille Militairc and the
Croix de Guerre.

Versailles, June 30.-World peace
was signed and sealed In the historic
hall of mirrors at Versailles June 2S,
what dimmed the expectations of
those who had worked and fought
during long years of war and months
of negotiations for its achievement.


Germany and the allied and asso-
ciated powers signed the peace terms
Ia the same imperial hall where the
Germans humbled the French so igno-
minously forty-eight years ago.


This formally ended the world war
which lasted just thirty-seven days
less than five years. Today, the day
Of peace, is the fifth anniversary Of
the murder of Archduke Frances
Ferdinand at Serajevo.


The ceremony of signing the peace
terms was brief. Premier Clemen-
ceau called the session to order in the
Hall of Mirrors of the Chateau of
Versailles at 3 10 o'clock The signing
began when DR.. Hermann Mueller
and Johannes Bell, the German sigma
tories, affixed their names.


The German correspondents were
ushered into the hall shortly before
8 o'clock and were given standing
correspondents section.


When Premier Lloyd George ar
rived many of the delegates sought
autographs from the members of the
council of four, and they busted them
selves signing copies of the official
program until the Germans entered
the room.


At o'clock a hush fell over the
hall and the crowds shouted for the
officials who were standing to sit
down so as not to block the view.
The delegates showed some surprise
at the disorder, which did not cease
until all spectators either had seated
themselves or found places against
the walls.


At seven minutes past 3 DR.. Her
mann Mueller, the German secretary
for foreign affairs, and DR.. Bell, the
colonial secretary, were shown into
the hall and quietly took seats at the
left end of the U-shaped table. They
showed composure and manifested
none of the uneasiness Count Won
Brockdorff- -Rantzau, head of the Ger
man peace delegation, displayed when
handed the treaty at Versailles.


NJ. Clemenceau, as president of the
conference, made brief speech in
viting the Germans to sign the treaty,
and there was a tense pause. Will
lam Martin, master of ceremonies,
after a moments delay, escorted the
German plenipotentaries to the sig
natory table, where they signed the
treaty, the protocol and the Polish
undertaking. Because of the confu-
sion and the crowd, the signing lost
much of its expected dignity.


After the Germans had signed,
President Wilson, followed by the
other American delegates, made his
way to the table and he and the
others speedily affixed their sigma
lures. Premier Lloyd George came
next with the English delegation. The
British dominions followed-Canada,
Australia, New Zealand, South Africa
and India in the order famed.


A murmur of surprise passed around
the hall when it became known that
General Smuts, representing South
Africa, signed under protest and filed
document declaring that the peace
was unsatisfactory.


NJ. Clemenceau, with the French
delegates, were the next in line for
the signing, and then Baron Saion1i
and the other japanese delegates. The
Italians came after the Japanese and
were followed by the representatives
of the smaller powers.


During the attaching of the sigma
lures of the great powers and the
Germans battery of moving picture
machines and cameras clicking away
could be heard above the general dis
order.


At AS o'clock the booming of can
non in celebration of the peace broke
the monotoEy in the hall of mirrors
where the crowd had tired of the al
most endless signing.

LONDON, March 22.-The first ac-
count of remarkable long distance
flight over the North Sea which was
performed by British nom rigid air.
ship, the US-11. during the last few
days is now officially published. The
voyage took the form of CIRCUIT, en-
bracing the coast Of Denmark, Schles
wig Holstein, Helgoland, North Ger

characterized by extremely unfavor-
able weather and therefore is regarded
as ranking as perhaps the most not
able flight of the kind ever undertaken.


The total length of the round trip
was ,2S5 air miles, and the time taken
was about forty and half hours.


The airship started from the Firth
of Forth, laying a straight course
toward Denmark. There was a north
west wind of fifteen to twenty miles
an hour and the night was dark, but
the airship was only mile from her
course when she passed the Dogger
Bank lighthouse. Then the wind in
creased and calcium flares were
dropped into the sea frequently to de-
termine the location.


i He diiSHlp 3 tTOuDleS began on the
return Journey The wind became
stronger and more tempestuous. At
midnight one engine became useless
and the ship was forced considerable
distance to leeward. The captain con-
templated landing in France, but
finally decided to hold on in the hope
the wind would abate. The wind abat-
ing somewhat, a "land fall" was made
at North Forel. At this time the
gasolene supply was running low and
only one engine could be kept run
ming.


During the last stage of the voy-
age the wind was very violent and the
crew had the greatest difficulty in con-
trolling the ship. All suffered in
tenscly from seasickness, especially
pilots and coxwains.


The fight was carried out entirely
over the sea. 1t was the longest non
stop overseas voyage ever made by
British air craft and so far as known

Cart with curtains and legend,
Through rains it has faded pale:

Gypsy wife in the doorway,


Her dark eyes eircled with woe,

Food for the mules and monkey,
Four children left to the last;
Mules may yet pull the wagon
Beyond the pitiless past.
Sat a-tilt in the byway,


Blue wisps from the chimney stream;
Fellows with sticks and pebbles,
Come hear the monkey scream!
Forty francs for monkey,


Now cringing under the wheel;
Children a-bed, a-dreaming


Above the monkeys squeal.
Fire of twigs for the cooking,


And supper for less than one,
Gypsy wife in the doorway,


Watching the setting sun.

France, June 6, 1918. Immediately
after the company in which Sergt.
Hoffman belonged had reached Its OBJ
jective on Hill 142, several counter-at-
tacks were launched against the line
before the new position had been con-
solidated. Sergt. Hoffman was at
tempting to organize a position on the
north slope of the hill when he saw
twelve. of the enemy, armed with five
light machine guns, crawling toward
his group. Giving the alarm, he rushed
at the hostile detachment, bayonetted
the two leaders, and forced the others
to flee, abandoning their guns. His
quick initiative and courage routed the
enemy from position from which they
could have swept the hill with machine
gun fire and forced the withdrawal of
our forces. His home is in Brooklyn.

BOSTON, April 16.-The Metropolitan

from New York for this city, collided
with bridge over the Cape Cod Canal
at Sycamore early to-day About twenty
feet of tine forward deck, including a
portion of the pilot house, was torn
away and three persons were injured.

believed to have been responsible for the
accident.

collision. One was a priest, who was
found buried beneath a pile of bedding
and debris when his stateroom was
reached.


After striking the bridge abutment
the steamer swung around and ran into
the canal bank in such a way as TO
block the waterway. Several vessels.
including the freight steamer Delaware.
bound for Boston. were waiting to pass
through the canal.


The Belfast was completing her first
round trip OF the season. She carried
$50 passengers.


r. o. Reed OF West Somerville. who
was the most seriously injured was
brought to a hospital here Physicians
said he had fractured rib and that one
lung was punctured.


Oficials of the Eastern Steamship
Lines announced that there would be
no sailings tonight either from New
York or Boston. The steamer Governor
Cobb will be put in place of the Belfast
tomorrow night and the Northland, now
at New York, would be held there until
tomorrow.

lack of Incoming persons who are not
immune to the disease.

months, owing to the energetic san-
tary measures. General Gorgas said
he could not be sure the plague was
cradle. ted there until after the close
of the rainy season. now beginning,
but he thought that the sanitary work
there was sufficient to prevent rein
fection bringing about the definite end
of the yellow fever menace, the first
of the great diseases to suffer eXtirpa-
tion.

Dark as the clouds even,
Ranked in the western heaven,
Waiting the breath that lifts
All the dread mass, and drifts
Tempest and falling brand
Over a ruined land


So still and orderly,


Arm to arm, knee to knee,
Waiting the great event,


Stands the black regiment.
Down the long dusky line
Teeth gleam and eyeballS shine;
And the bright bayonet,
Bristling and firmly set,
Flashed with purpose grand,
Long ere the sharp command
OF the fierce rolling drum
Told them their time had come,
Told them what work was sent
For the black regiment.


Now" the flag-sergeant cried,

If we are fit to be

Down, like the whining hound

oh, what shout there went

Bayonet and saber stroke

Leaping with open hands,

Whether for veal or woe;
Glad to breathe one free breath,

Praying-alas in vain

So they could once more see
That burst to liberty!
This was what freedom" lent

The King and Mr.. Wilson then re-
at the station, while The band played
THE Star-Spangled Banner" After a
short conversation in the royal waiting
room, the King and Mr.. Wilson ap-
peared in front of the station. This
was a signal for great outburst of
enthusiasm, cannons being fired, SOL
diers presenting arms and the historic
bell on the Capitol ringing, which is
done only on greatest national occa
sions.


At the Plaza Eseara, Prince Prospero
Colonna, the Mayor Of Rome, surround
ed by Aldermen and liveried servants,
awaited the arrival of the procession.
Prince Colonna delivered an address, in
which he welcomed the President in
the name of the Eternal City and eX-
pressed the gratitude of Rome and
Italy for all America did materially
and spiritually to win the war.


This imposing scene occurred in the
huge square bounded on one side by
the venerable ruins of the Diocletian
baths and on the other by scmicircular
buildings gayly decorated with palms,
flowers and streamers bearing the
names of redeemed Italian cities. The
moment Prince Colonna's address was
over the cheering broke forth once
more with redoubled vigor


Smile Causes Ovation


The procession turned down the Via
Nazionale, long, straight thorough
fare leading almost directly to the
Quirinal. The smile of the President
caused an ovation, which became more
tremendous as he drove along From
windows flowers were showered upon
Mrs. Wilson and Miss Wilson. They
acknowledged the peoples salutatons,
their bows producing even greater out
bursts of enthusiasm.


The King and the President drove in
the same carriage, with the Queen and
Mrs. Wilson in the next.


When the Presidential party arrived
at the Quirinal the military bugles
blared forth and the guard Of honor
presented arms, while the square, al
ready full, became packed to its capac-
ity with the streams of humanity pour
ing in from all sides and calling loudly
for Preside Wilson to appear on the
balcony


The President and Mrs Wilson, to-
gether with their royal hosts, respond
ed to the call. The sight of them on
the balcony was the signal for the eli
max of the demonstration. The crowd
seemed completely to have lost it's
senses, the people cheering unres train
edly for President Wilson and for
America. The Presidential party was
obliged to appear several times on the
balcony to satisfy the clamors of the
people.


Reception Inside Palace


When President Wilson and his party
reached the Quirinal from the railway
station they were conducted inside the
palace to the Throne Room, where there
was an informal reception. Mrs. Wilson
and Queen Helena chatted for few
moments while the President talked
earnestly with King Victor Emmanuel,
Premier Orlando and others. The mas
sive staircases were lined with the
young men of the Kings Household
Guard.


President and Mrs. Wilson later took
luncheon with the royal family at the
Villa Savoy, which is just outside the
walls of the city, standing in magni-
ficent park.

Police Headquarters III Brooklyn was

aged, but the lights in the telegraph

blown out fuse could be replaced.


The rain descended upon the borough

filling the cellars of stores and block

over the sidewalks, flooding many eel
lars.

Coney Island was plunged into dark
ness that was almost complete for an
hour. Lightning struck an Edison Com
pany feed wire, blowing out fuses. in
the plant near the West End depot,
and dousing every light al the resort
except those. getting current from in
dependent plants. Visitors 10 the re
sort were marooned on scenic railways,
Ferris wheels and carrouscls, while
lightning blazed about them and rain
drenched them.


From $40 to 10:40 p. m, except for
two intervals Of about two minutes
each, the only electric lights on the
island were those on the B. r. I. cars
and trains and on autos. Few of the
theatres, movie houses and restaurants
are equipped with gas, and, save where
ioresl lghted prOprIetorS had laid in
candles, the patrons had TO either sit
patiently, IN the dark or grope their
way to the streets.


Persons on the sidewalks collided
with one another frequently, but there
was little real disorder. Luna Park.
Steeplechase. Henderson's Music Hall,
the New Brighton Theatre and other
resorts were crowded when the lights
went out

on the top floor of the Coney Island
police station and ran pelmel for the
stairs when the lights went out. Cap
tam Byron Sackett, commander of the
precinct, met them halfway down and
led them out into the rain


Candles replaced incandescents at the
Brighton Theatre and the show went
on, the audience remaining seated and
unperturbod. The sudden storm drove
an abnormal crowd to the West End
depot, but there was no sign of panic
there, the lights, which are fed from
the b. X. 7. power house, remaining
brilliant

not only Coney Island, but Brighton

street, and robbed the cash drawer of
$40 after beating the clerk into un-
consciousness carly yesterday morning.
The thugs bound the clerk to a chair
and then gagged him. They overlooked
$4,000 in a drawer.


John Cullen, the night clerk. SAYS the
men got close to him under pretext of
finding out the time. Two of them
covered him with revolvers. while the
third jumped the counter separating him
from the trio. The latter, who bore a
big scar on his left cheek, demanded to
know where the money was kept. After
Cullen pointed out the petty cash
drawer he was knocked unconscious by
a violent blow behind the ear.


In their hurry the bandits made no
effort to find any money other than that
designated by Cullen. AS result thew
overlooked the larger amount in an ad-
Joining compartment. Cullen's pockets
were searched and several dollars were
taken.


The clerk recovered consciousness in
time to see the three men escaping
through rear window. They had bound
and gagged him, however, and he could
make no outcry until some time later
when his assistant returned from his
midnight supper and released him.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa, Nov. IL
Three men were killed and a dozen
persons were injured when the tug
Caspian crashed into the Atlantic
City, a Philadelphia and Reading
ferryboat playing between Camden,
N. j., and Philadelphia, early today.
All of the dead are unidentified.


Some of the injured were thrown
into the river, and were picked up
by boats which put out from the
shore. They were taken to various
piers along the Delaware and placed
on the docks, from where they were
hurried to hospitals in patrol wagons.


Police believe the list of both the
dead and the injured may be in
creased. The ferry was heavily load
ed with workmen coming from New
Jersey on their way to work, many
of them bound for the Hog Island
shipyard.


The dead were crushed almost be-
yond recognition. Two of those
killed are said to have met death
when the tug crashed into the ferry
boat, and they were thrown into the
water. The ferry became almost un-
manageable. She tried to back away
and two of the Injured are said to
have been sucked into the paddle
wheel, where the life was crushed
from them.


Just how the tug came to ram the
Terry has not been ascertained, as the
weather was clear and the ferry
should have been clearly discernibie.

PARIS, Oct. 21.-King Alfonso OF
Spain arrived in Paris yesterday and
began almost Immediately to carry
out the program arranged for his
brief stay in the city before he pro-
ceeds to England. Arriving at the
Quai dOrsay station. the monarch
was welcomed by Stephen Pichon.
French foreign minister; Colonel
Badet, representing President Poin-
care: Senior de Leon, Spanish ambas-
sador. and others.


Alfonso wore civilian clothes, and,
dressed in a light gray overcoat and
wearing soft fedora hat and a soft
collar. presented an appearance which
contrasted sharply with that of the
French officials and the Spanish
grandees, who were dressed in the
regulation frock coats, and wore silk
hats. Crowds gathered outside the
station in the heavy fog. and chered
Alfonso as he emerged from the sta
ton.


In the afternoon Alfonso paid visits
to President Poincare, Premier Glenn
enceau, and Foreign Minister Piehon.

FERGUS FALLS, Mimi. June 23-
Between sixty and seventy persons
were killed and more than a hundred
were badly injured by the tornado
terday and tore a large section of the
city, including the business district. to
pieces. Thirty eight bodies have been
recovered.


State troops began searching the
wreckage shortly after daylight. 1t is
believed that more than dozen
bodies are buried in the debris which
was the Grand Hotel. Fifty persons
were in this building when the tor
nado came About thirty Of them are
dead


Much of the residence district south
of the Red river is a waste.
Stores and Dwellings Demolished.


About 500 stores and residences were
demolished A score or more Of per-
sons are missing. The property loss
is estimated at several million dol
lars. Virtually the entire north
western section of the city is in ruins.
Public buildings and churches were
destroyed. Hospitals are crowded
with victims. but city officials said
this morning they believed Fergus
Falls would be able to provide relief
for it's sufferers.


Citizens said they believe that three
storms struck the city in quick sue
cession. Several persons corroborated
statements that three funnel shaped
clouds were seen. The first apparently
struck the town from the northwest
and tore through the Lake Alice dis
trict. This smash wrecked the
Grand Hotel The second cloud
brought driving rain and approached
from the southwest. The third swept
over the eastern section from the
southeast.

Atlanta, Ga, Dec. 12-After having
done damage estimated at several
million dollars the floods which start
ed this week in Georgia, Alabama
and Mississippi were slowly receding
tonight Many cities. however. were
stin flooded and industries paralyzed.
This condition applied especially to
those places on rivers which did not
start to rise the first two or three
days.


Montgomery. Ala. probably was the
h&rdest hit Of any of the cities in the
hood area. Street car service Is at
an absolute standstill. the power sta
tions having been flooded. The pub
lie schools have been closed to save
heat and light. The river has over
flowed into the city's artesian well
system. and Mayor Gunter has
warned Of the menace that exists II
the water Is drunk unless II Is first
boiled. The crest of the flood has
been reached. and the river tonight
appeared to be slowly receding.


Many persons were marooned
around the city. but only five lives
were lost. according to latest re-
ports. The toll of human life was
generally small through the three
States.


Train service still was badly de-
moralized in lower Alabama. Mis-
sissippi and Georgia Railroads
suffered heavily from washouts
and Industries from their plants
being flooded. Farmers lost hun
dreds of head of livestock and the
southern portions suffered from
damage to growing crops.

VERSAILLES, May In session.
beginning at $40 o'clock this after
noon and lasting barely five minutes,
the German plenipotentiaries of the
peace congress presented their ere
dentials. 1t was the first step in the
peace negotiations. The German ere
dentials were presented to repre-
sentatives of the allies and the Unit
ed States.


Pale and almost fainting from emo
ton, Count Won Brockdorff- Rantzau.
the German foreign secretary and
head of the delegation, passed
through what evidently was one of
the bitterest moments of his life. He
was barely able to sustain himself
through the brief ceremony and reach
the waiting automobile. which had
brought him to the gathering.


The meeting took place in the room
of the Trianon Hotel previously used
for the sessions of the supreme mill
tary council. Count Won Brockdorff
Rantzau on entering. was accom-
panied by Herr Landsberg, Prof
Schuecking and two secretaries. and
waiting for him the allied representa-
tives were grouped around Jules
Cambon, the former French ambassa-
dor to Berlin, who is chairman of the
commission.


Other members of the allied party
included Henry White of the United
States, Lord Harding of Great Britain
and Ambassador Matsui, Japan.

der the embargo. Nothing which has hap
pened for a generation has aroused the
horticultural interests Of the country as
this curious ruling, the reason for which
lies in the expressed belief that there is
danger of introducing insect pests or fun
gus diseases. There are some professional
growers who support the board in its posi-

WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, w. Va.
Aug. 16-Whte Sulphur Springs has
never known more successful August,
with both the Greenbrler and The
White packed to capacity and cottagers
harborlng many friends who have come
for the great social weeks of August.
The crowd has been so heavy that the
rest rooms in the bath establishment
have been converted into sleeping
quarters, and surrounding resorts have
cared for many motor parties unable
to receive accomm odations here. Co
tillons are being revived at the Old
White this season. and the horse show
cotillon Friday night was great sue
cess, over 800 people dancing in the
famous old ballroom and about that
many forming an interested gallery.


The horse show at The Meadows was
the chief attraction this last week, as
it always is, and receipts at the gate
showed the largest attendance in the
history of the show. Many motor par
ties came from Charleston. Hot

points across the mountains.

shows and at Madison Square

oh hat hac

PARIS. Jan. 21.-Food conditions
throughout the Balkan peninsula are
so terrible that all of the larger
European powers and the United
States are bending every effort to al
leviate the distressing conditions.
Though great privations were sur
fered during the long period of actual
warfare, conditions prevailing today
are far worse.


During the past year but little was
grown on cultivable lands. Often
times peasants have been in too
emaciated a condition even to work
such little plots as they may have
possessed, and it is estimated that
tens of thousands of acres of land
which might have produced supplies
to increase national larders were not
planted and titled because peoples
under the press of hunger ate grains
and seeds which had been saved for
last years crops.


Though food difficulties have been
and still are extremely grave, the
same may be said of other living con-
ditions. Peoples throughout the
Balkans are existing in abject
squaIor. Light and heat have become
almost things of the past. Owing to
the lack of fuel in most homes, con-
sumption has made rapid inroads,
while other diseases have increased
proportionately.

Swinging by ono hand from an over
hanging cornice, Patrolman Frank
Centner yesterday rescued four per-
sons who had been trapped by fire
on the top floor of 80 Monitor Street
Brooklyn. The blaze started in the
cellar, where Mrs. Catherine Berick
seventy, was sorting some old clothes
by the light of candle. How it
started will never be known, for the
woman was burned to death


On the top floor of the frame build
ing Harry and Loretta Ward and their
children, Harry, two years old, and
John, baby, were trapped by flames
and dazed by smoke. The elder Wards
prepared to jump to the street. three
floors below. Centner shouted at them
to stay where they were

floor of an adjoining house and made

around projecting water pipe to the
Wards front room. From there he
carried the children and the mother
and father. Centner is attached to the
Herbert Street station. The house
burned to the ground The charred
body of Mrs. Berick was found in the
basement.


From the smoke-fled two-story
frame tenement, at 262 North Tenth
Street, Brooklyn, Patrolmen McDer-
mott, Williams, Green and Plunkitt, of
the Bedford Avenue station, rescued
Mrs. Lillia Tosarno and her eight chill
dren. Firemen and the four patrolmen
then went to the upper part of the
building and rescued James Aldorofe
his wife, Rosa, and their four chill
dren. Other patrolmen saved Tony
Carmilo, his wife, Angelina and their
two children, and the Cainetti family
of four, who were brought down on
ladders.


All concerned were treated for smoke
suffocation, but none was injured seri
ously.


The fire destroyed the garage at 26(
North Tenth Street, where it origi
mated, and with it went twenty auto.
mobiles.

surprising strength. Stocks forced on

ing until 1880 at which time enough

onnoiter the ground beyond, was sud

gun, rushed forward with his bayonet
fixed, through wheat field toward

right leg nearly severed above the
knee, and with several bullet holes in
his body, with undaunted courage, he
continued to fire into the emplace-
ment from a prone position, killing
two of the enemy and dispensing the
rest of the crew. Private Dilboy's
home was in Boston, Mass.

rive their name from the fact that

several years ago was much smaller

A'A Vests voice rose in shrill

like that!" And she burst into tears.
Long after, when Virginia had coaxed
her to sleep and lay awake by her
mothers side listening to the countless
little night noises outside and worry
ing as no girl of eighteen should about
the future, there came at last the
conviction that the future was no
longer to- be accepted passively as she
had accepted it all her life. Life was
hers now to live for herself, and there
was something glorious in the thought,
ignorant and frightened as she was.
With this realization she dropped
asleep.


Mrs. West was still asleep the next
morning when Virginia opened her
eyes. She slept like child, and Vir-
ginia lay looking at her for a long
time. She felt great enveloping ten
derness for her mother. 1t wasn't her
fault, any of it--used to luxury all
her life, as she had been, and with
no idea of how to use money. Virginia
thought of the useless extravagances
which she might have helped to avoid if
she had known the truth, ard wondered
what her mother would do without the
things about her that meant not luxury
now, but just the necessities of daily
living.


She ordered breakfast upstairs and
telephoned down to the Office that they
were giving up their rooms. When
the breakfast came she carried it to
her mother, and they ate together from
a little table pulled up close to the
side of the bed. The room was already
strewn with their belongings and two
large trunks were standing open in the
next room all ready to be packed.


Mrs. West was listless and depressed.
She consented to Virginias plan to
leave Immediately simply because there
seemed nothing else to do. In one day
Virginia had emerged from under her
mothers wing and was taking the reins
of government into her own hands.
Yesterday she had been a child, taking
without question what her mother gave
her. Today she was engineering their
departure, paying their bills with
money from her mothers pocketbook
She was more thankful for the fact
that there was enough money there
Ahan she had ever been for anything
before in her life.


They left the hotel without seeing
Sherman Holmes, and Virginia, who
had managed everything, broke down
when they were finally seated in the
train, and wept into her handkerchief
like frightened child. The glory that
she had felt the night before had de-
parted. She was facing reality now,
and it was very different from just
speculating about life from a safe van
tage point.


Virginia had telegraphed Jimmy that
morning, and when she reached home
an answer was waiting for her. Jimmy
would be in town Saturday. A little
ray of comfort stole into her heart with
this assurance. She did not feel quite
so alone. A thick envelope containing
letter from Kathleen was also wait
ing for her, and she sat down in the
unaired living room with her hat and
coat still on to read it. Mrs. West
was not depressed to the extent of neg
1ecting her looks in any way. She
was already in her room repairing the
ravages that the train trip had caused,
cold creaming her face and slipping
into soft negligee. These things were
as natural to her as getting UP i'll the
morning; she even hummed little tune
while she drew the comb through the
waves of her hair.


Kathleen's letter was full of excite
ment. She had met wealthy man,
who had invited her to a party on his
yacht; but he was old and she couldn' t
make up her mind to marry him. She
had missed Virginia, but that was over
now, as she and her mother were COM
ing to New York next week.


"We'll have some gay times this
winter with no rules to worry about

you forgotten your. fooiishness with
jimmy? I hope SO. You ought to
marry some one with plenty of money"


Virginia let the letter fall into her
lap. For time she had forgotten all
about Kathleen.

fearing injury of persons not implicated
in the attack.


The ambuscade is the first overt act
that has been committed against either
regular soldiers or Indiana militiamen
since troops were sent to Gary.

les Vertes," more than 10000 feet high.

where they suffered terrible expert
ences. The men were hungry and
frozen and were compelled to slip and
slide down precipices, as they were
wearing boots without nails They
became lost among the pnnacles and
peaks.


One of the Hungarians fell into a
crevice and was killed. Another, who
was injured, managed to crawl into
the village of Bourg, from which place
twelve Alpinists and guides set out to
search for the other three men. One
was discovered half frozen, but no
trace could be found of the other two.
These men are believed to have lost
their lives, but the search for them is
continuing. The Hungarians said that
they had never climbed mountains be-
fore. They declared their only idea
was to walk northwards toward liberty.
